📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, utah has sued the companies behind the Stake sweepstakes site, alleging it ran an illegal casino for Utahns since 2022. The case follows Florida's own suit against Stake and adds to the legal pressure on the dual-currency sweepstakes model.

It has been revealed that the timing of Utah’s suit against Stake stands out. Stake added Utah to its list of restricted states on Nov. 13, four days before the suit was filed, yet state consumer protection investigators could still use the site as recently as Nov. 16, when a banner said access would end on Dec. 7, the 43-page complaint claims.

Utah Attorney General Derek Brown and the Utah Department of Commerce’s Division of Consumer Protection brought the case. It names two defendants: Sweepsteaks Limited, based in Cyprus, and its Australian parent, Easygo Group Holdings Pty Ltd. The state refers to them jointly as Stake.

The central allegation is that Stake has offered Utahns a round-the-clock casino since 2022. Utah has prohibited gambling since it became a state, and its Constitution bans gambling.

The complaint takes aim at how the site works. Players spend real money on two virtual currencies.

Utah wants the court to declare the site illegal gambling under state law. It also asks the court to bar Stake from offering its games in Utah and to order the firm to return money taken from residents. The state is also seeking fines under the Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act and a remedy for harm to the public. The complaint adds claims for unjust enrichment, public nuisance and declaratory judgment.

A demand that players’ losses be repaid raises the stakes for the wider industry. Taken together, the relief Utah seeks increases the legal risk for sweepstakes operators, suppliers and affiliates nationwide.

Recent findings suggest that utah is not the only state to bring Stake itself into court. Florida’s suit is broader in scope. It names Sweepsteaks Ltd and Easygo alongside Medium Rare and Kick Streaming, NEXT.io reported. It also names co-founders Bijan Tehrani and Ed Craven, plus payment firms Praxis and Breeze Labs Payments. Utah’s complaint is limited to the two corporate defendants.

Recent findings suggest that other states have targeted the same business model through a different operator. Kentucky and Arkansas have both sued VGW, which runs its own dual-currency sweepstakes sites.

The Stake case is separate from Utah’s clash with federal regulators over prediction markets. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has sued Utah to stop the state from using its own laws to shut down CFTC-registered contract markets. The Stake suit also came less than three weeks after Utah filed criminal charges against Kalshi’s founders. Those charges include felony counts of online gambling promotion.

Court records did not list a lawyer for either defendant, and the company did not answer a request for comment on the suit.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • To help developers put Hydrogen to work, today we're launching the Robotics plugin on Google Antigravity: a set of skills for hardware onboarding, simulation and robot control turning Antigravity into a one-stop robotics workbench.

Sources indicate that over the past month, Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 4 Carbon brought frontier physical reasoning to robotics: understanding 3D scenes, reconstructing real environments in simulation, practicing tasks in sim before running them on hardware, and directly controlling robot arms from camera images. Last week, we introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen, which brings strong spatial and embodied reasoning to a much faster model built for speed and efficiency.

To help developers put Hydrogen to work, today we're launching the Robotics plugin on Google Antigravity: a set of skills for hardware onboarding, simulation and robot control turning Antigravity into a one-stop robotics workbench. Together, they enable a developer to go from a robot in a box to one that can perform a working application in an afternoon. To install the plugin, open Antigravity, go to Customizations and search for Robotics on the Build With Google shelf.

Gemini 4 Argon and Carbon revealed that a general model can drive a robot arm directly, and Gemini 4 Hydrogen preserves that ability. Give it a goal in plain language and a camera view, and it prepares the task, writes and runs the control code, and keeps adjusting until the job is done. On the Artificial Analysis Robotics 0.1 benchmark, Gemini 4 Hydrogen controls a real 6-axis arm through eight everyday tabletop tasks, from pouring a drink to packing blocks into a box. Hydrogen scores 58, similar to Argon at a lower cost per token.

Hydrogen brings the specialized skills of our Gemini Robotics ER 2 (Embodied Reasoning) models into the core Gemini 4 model series, and it beats them on nearly every axis. On the public ERQA benchmark, Hydrogen outperforms Gemini Robotics ER 2 on spatial reasoning tasks such as multi-view correspondence and 3D trajectory reasoning. For developers using Gemini Robotics ER 2 today, we recommend trying out Gemini 4 Hydrogen for these workloads.

#138478. GPU Management: Why Idle GPUs Are the Newly introduced Grounded Aircraft

GPU Management: Why Idle GPUs Are the Newly introduced Grounded Aircraft

📅 30 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2659 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For most of the industry's history, the number that best predicted whether an airline would survive was how much of the day each aircraft spent on the ground.
  • Industry observers note that the reason is structural.
  • According to recent reports, A bigger fleet still helps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Aviation learned this the hard way. For most of the industry's history, the number that best predicted whether an airline would survive was how much of the day each aircraft spent on the ground.

Industry observers note that the reason is structural. An aircraft's costs accrue by the calendar hour: financing, depreciation, hull insurance, scheduled maintenance, crew contracts. Its revenue accrues only by the flight hour. Every hour spent on the ground shrinks the output side of that equation while the cost side keeps running exactly as before. Utilization also sits downstream of almost everything else an airline does. Turnaround discipline, network design, maintenance planning, crew rostering, and spare parts availability all eventually show up in that one number, because a broken operation underneath it keeps planes on the ground no matter what else goes right.

According to recent reports, A bigger fleet still helps. More aircraft means more available capacity, plainly and simply. But two airlines flying comparable fleets on comparable routes can end up with very different economics, and most of that gap traces back to one measurement rather than fleet size.

Enterprise AI is running into the same structure, on a different piece of hardware. A GPU accrues cost by the calendar hour too, through financing, depreciation, power, and cooling, whether or not it's doing anything useful in a given moment. Its output only accrues by the compute hour. More GPUs helps in roughly the way a bigger fleet helps an airline: real capacity, a genuine advantage, and still no guarantee of the result that actually decides who wins. Two companies with comparable GPU budgets increasingly diverge based on how much of that hardware is doing something useful at any given moment, not on how much of it either one owns. That same number, like an airline's utilization rate, sits downstream of nearly every other infrastructure decision a company makes. Intelligence has carried the industry this far. Utilization is where the next real constraint is forming.

The scarcity didn't disappear as AI scaled. It moved up the chain, landing on a different resource entirely.

The first wave of enterprise AI was won on model quality. Bigger models, trained on more compute, evaluated against tougher benchmarks: parameter count and leaderboard position dominated the conversation, and the race produced models genuinely good enough to run real enterprise workloads. That capability arrives bundled with a dependency, though. Production AI runs on specialized hardware, and today that hardware is almost entirely GPUs.

In a recent development, GPUs are expensive, supply constrained, and in demand far beyond what's available, and this holds even at the very top of the market. In 2020, Microsoft built OpenAI a dedicated supercomputer: over 10,000 GPUs and 285,000 CPU cores, reported at the time as one of the five largest systems in the world, assembled to train what became GPT-3. At the time, it looked like an almost unimaginable concentration of hardware, the kind of number that made compute look like a solved problem for whoever could get access to it. Six years later, that number reads more like a starting point than a ceiling. By 2026, even the best capitalized labs on the planet were treating compute access as a live strategic constraint rather than a settled one. Anthropic alone was running simultaneous multi-gigawatt commitments across four separate hardware platforms, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and AMD, layered within months of one another, while Meta signed a comparable multi-gigawatt deal of its own. Spreading commitments across four vendors at once is what compute scarcity looks like when a buyer has effectively unlimited capital and still can't get enough from any single source.

It has been revealed that six years apart, both events marked the frontier of what a lab needed just to stay competitive. What changed in between has less to do with AI getting more capable, and everything to do with capability no longer being the binding constraint.

The same pattern highlights up downstream of the labs, in a different form. Enterprises consuming these models through an API run into a pricing problem more than a hardware one. Cost scales linearly with tokens used, and that single fact separates the economics of a proof of concept from the economics of production almost completely. A PoC processing a few thousand requests a month looks affordable. The same workload at production volume can turn into a cost line that never quite clears. The alternative gaining ground is straightforward enough: enterprises acquiring their own GPUs and running models locally, trading a variable, linearly scaling cost for a fixed capital one.

API cost rises with usage, while owned infrastructure stays close to fixed. Past the breakeven point, the trade reverses.

That shift turns the GPU into infrastructure rather than a line item, sized for growth, sized for demand peaks, and therefore sized above what any given week actually needs. Which means the purchase doesn't close the problem. It opens a new one. The day the cluster comes online, the question stops being can we get accelerators and becomes can we keep them busy, and only the first question had a procurement team assigned to it. Signing for the hardware is the part with a deadline and an owner. Keeping it off the ground is the part that quietly decides whether the deal was worth signing.

In a recent development, these deals describe capacity commitments, not efficiency. How well that capacity gets used is a separate question, owned by different people, measured far less rigorously, and considerably further from being solved.

In a recent development, A cluster full of busy GPUs can still be wasting most of its potential, and the reason is almost always the same one. GPUs run continuously, day and night, while the demand placed on them does not. Infrastructure has to be sized for the peak, the moment training runs, batch jobs, and real time traffic all land at once, which leaves a meaningful share of capacity provisioned and unused outside that peak. Better forecasting could solve that on its own if every GPU could absorb every kind of work equally well. Few can, and that turns out to be the harder half of the problem.

The mismatch begins one layer deeper.

Industry observers note that in the first generation of enterprise AI, a GPU's job was largely singular: run inference. Today the same hardware supports training, fine-tuning, quantization, real-time inference, batch inference, embedding generation, and model evaluation, often for the same organization, sometimes for the same model, on the same cluster. Each of these workloads wants something different from the hardware, and the differences run deep. Real-time inference needs low latency above nearly everything else, because a slow response counts as a failed one. Batch work cares about throughput and tolerates delay, sometimes for hours. Training can occupy a GPU continuously for a stretch measured in hours or days. Quantization needs a large amount of capacity, but only briefly. A scheduler tuned for one of these will misallocate the other three almost by default. The failure doesn't always show up on a utilization dashboard either. A cluster can report high average occupancy while several queued jobs wait for a GPU shape that happens to be busy running something else entirely.

Industry observers note that the exact workload mix varies by organization. The shape of the problem does not. This is also where the aircraft analogy runs into its limit, and the limit teaches something rather than just qualifying the comparison. An idle aircraft can usually be redeployed to any route in the fleet: a 737 sitting in Chicago can fly to Denver instead of Dallas without much penalty. An idle GPU can only absorb a workload whose memory, latency, and duration profile it can actually serve. That difference makes orchestration harder than fleet scheduling, and it's why the question stops being whether GPUs are occupied and turns into which workload should run on which GPU, at what time, with what priority. Buying another rack of GPUs adds capacity and cost, not a fix for the mismatch, and that newly introduced capacity can sit in the wrong shape at the wrong moment just as easily as the capacity already installed.

Sources indicate that maximizing GPU ROI takes more than a one-time provisioning decision. It calls for continuous, active management of the infrastructure itself, running every hour rather than only at procurement time. What's emerging in response is a distinct discipline, GPU Management, an orchestration layer sitting between workloads, models, and hardware. Its job is to decide, continuously, which workload runs, when it runs, how it runs, and on which specific GPU in the cluster. None of this is exotic in concept. It's closer to what a good operations team already does by instinct, just formalized and running continuously instead of depending on someone noticing a problem.

Intelligence doesn't stop at the model boundary. The orchestration layer is making real-time allocation decisions the model itself has no visibility into.

Intelligence used to sit almost entirely in the model: bigger, better trained, more capable, and that was most of the game. Now it also has to sit in the infrastructure, in the layer deciding, moment to moment, which of several competing workloads gets the GPU that just freed up, and at what priority relative to everything else waiting in the queue. Keeping GPUs busy stops being the goal on its own, since busy is easy to fake by running low priority work that could have waited. Maximizing the return generated by each installed GPU becomes the actual target, and that turns out to be a far more continuous problem than the provisioning question that came before it.

According to recent reports, provisioning well doesn't make this go away so much as change its shape. A provisioning decision gets made once, at purchase time. An allocation decision gets made constantly: every time a job finishes, every upcoming request that arrives, every shift in priority between a customer facing service and an internal training run. That frequency explains why the decision has moved from something a person handles case by case into something that has to run automatically. No engineer is watching a dashboard at three in the morning to decide whether a finished training run should hand its GPU to a queued batch job or hold it for an incoming burst of customer traffic. Something else has to make that call, continuously, and make it correctly often enough that nobody needs to check.

According to recent reports, the discipline is upcoming enough that its tooling and conventions are still forming, and no single playbook has emerged yet for what a mature GPU Management practice looks like. What has settled, at least, is where the constraint moved.

Specialization and orchestration solve different halves of the same problem.

Specialized, smaller models can perform specific tasks at a fraction of the resource cost a large generalist model would need for the same job, without giving up the quality the task requires. That has a direct effect on utilization. Workloads that once required a single, large model, occupying a large share of a cluster's capacity for the full duration of the job, can instead run on smaller, task-specific models occupying a fraction of that footprint. Capacity that used to be entirely spoken for is suddenly free.

How much capacity specialization frees varies by workload and model, but the freed capacity still has to go somewhere or it just sits there. A smaller specialized model only converts into GPU ROI if something is actively deciding what happens next with the space it frees up, reallocating it to another workload, another model, another queue waiting behind it. Left unmanaged, freed capacity becomes a different flavor of idle rather than a win, invisible in a different way than an obviously unused GPU, but no more productive.

In a recent development, specialization without orchestration frees capacity nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming. Neither lever does the whole job alone.

Sources indicate that specialization without orchestration frees capacity that nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming in the first place, because the models are still large and the footprint they leave behind is small. Neither lever does the whole job alone; each one raises the ceiling on what the other lever can achieve. Neither is optional if the goal is to actually close the gap between installed capacity and useful output, rather than shifting where the waste happens to sit.

This is why model architecture and GPU management are two ways to address the same problem, approached from two different directions that end up leaning on each other. One shrinks what each workload needs. The other decides, continuously, where the difference goes.

A bigger fleet has always been a real advantage, and nothing here argues otherwise. Among airlines with comparable fleets, sometimes even a smaller one facing a larger rival, the winner was usually whichever one flew what it had more completely, carrying the weight of everything the airline did well underneath it. Enterprise AI is arriving at the same discipline from a different direction. GPUs are already installed, already depreciating, already committed. Specialized models and GPU Management are parallel solutions, or bivalent strategies. Specialization shrinks what each workload needs. Management maximizes the return on infrastructure. Enterprises that master both will set the pace of AI competition for the next decade.

Explore Dharma AI on Hugging Face to try our interactive demos, download our open-source models, and discover how specialized AI systems outperform general-purpose models in real enterprise applications.

The next frontier is managing an entire fleet of agents and there is nothing stopping it.

It has been revealed that agreed. And the part that isn't priced in yet: a fleet of agents makes per-token cost scale linearly with the business. At some point large enterprises stop paying that curve and bring the models in-house — which doesn't remove the cost, it just trades a vendor price list for a utilization number. And agent fleets are brutal on utilization: real-time inference under latency SLAs, batch jobs, retraining, evals — all bursty, all fighting over the same finite pool. Managing the fleet is going to be, in large part, a GPU scheduling problem.

Scheduling is the core bottleneck of this problem. A CPU-like isolation mechanism, or a sandbox-based architecture on GPUs, could significantly alleviate this issue.

Good point, isolation is a real part of the picture. CPU-style boundaries (and the GPU sandboxing now landing, like the Kata Containers work) are what make it safe to co-locate unrelated workloads on the same card without fault or memory-contention risk, which widens the set of placements a scheduler is even allowed to make.

It has been revealed that taking that a step further: once co-location is safe, we have to decide which workload runs on which GPU, at what time, at what priority, given that each one wants something different from the hardware (memory footprint, latency tolerance, duration). Isolation gives you a bigger, safer decision space; something still has to pick the right point in it. And rigid partitioning can even cut utilization, since an idle slice can't lend capacity to a busy neighbor.

In a recent development, that's exactly the direction we're taking next: an intelligent solution for job scheduling. We've got a follow-up article on it in the works, which will be published next week. Would be curious to get your read when it's out.

Sources indicate that I expect we will see GPU rental systems become a thing. There are a lot of high-end GPUs sitting in consumer computers doing absolutely nothing for 90% of the day. Imagine if individuals could allow a training model to access their GPU remotely and in return pay them something in return. Yes, remote GPUs is not optimal, but with the consumer taking on the maintenance, power bill, and ownership of the GPU, any use the training model gets is a net positive.

Motorola has been content with mid-grade haptics for years, but the Motorola Signature 27’s haptics rightfully upgrade the experience.

It has been revealed that two days ago, I unboxed the Motorola Signature 27 and talked about my experience a bit in my Motorola Signature 27 hands-on. It’s as gorgeous as the pictures make it look, and the texture on the back of my “Capulet Olive” green colorway is the stuff of dreams. But the thing that sealed the latest ultra-high-quality design for me wasn’t the comfortable curved edges or the textile back: it was the haptic motors.

Now, don’t get me wrong. The Motorola Signature 27’s build and design are probably my favorite of the year. I’ll need to use it for just a bit longer to be 100% sure, but the pebble-like aesthetic of the curved front, back, and edges feels tangibly amazing to hold and use. It reminds me a bit of the Galaxy S3’s design, just without the nasty, slimy plastic back. It’s curved just enough to feel amazing, but not enough to be an annoyance like some waterfall display phones were in the past.

According to recent reports, but a haptic motor is completely intangible to you as the reader. You can’t see it in pictures, and even if I describe it, you may not fully understand why it makes such a difference. If you’ve been using Google Pixel phones for a long time, you’ve probably forgotten how good a quality haptic motor can feel, but let me remind you for a moment just how important such an invisible thing can be to completing the experience.

According to recent reports, for photographers, videographers and content creators, an SD card is more than a storage device. It holds the raw material behind a finished project: wedding photographs, travel footage, product demos and drone recordings that may be impossible to recreate. Data loss can happen at almost any stage of that workflow, from a folder deleted to make space to a card formatted before the footage was backed up.

This article explains why files on a card become unavailable, what to do in the first minutes, how recovery tools find data, and how to compare options. It includes a small Python example that recovers JPEG files from a disk image, so you can see the mechanism for yourself. Recovery is never guaranteed, and tool features change, so confirm details against each vendor’s current documentation.

Industry observers note that recovery is not just a matter of finding a deleted filename. Several different problems can make files unavailable, and they call for different approaches.

These steps cannot guarantee recovery, but they reduce avoidable risk.

In a recent development, carving has a cost. Because file system information is ignored, names and folder structure are usually lost, which is why scan results often show generic names. Fragmented files can also be recovered incomplete, since the tool assumes the pieces are stored one after another. Free tools build on these same ideas. Wondershare Recoverit V15, which also offers a free version for Windows and Mac, adds a graphical interface, while PhotoRec and ddrescue stay closer to the command line.

Industry observers note that the script below is a teaching sketch, not a recovery product. It reads a raw disk image, finds JPEG start markers, and writes out the bytes up to the last end marker before the next start. That detail matters because a JPEG can contain an embedded thumbnail with its own markers, so stopping at the first end marker would cut a file short.

A short test builds two real JPEGs, hides them in random bytes, and checks that both are carved and open as valid images:.

Use it on an image rather than the card itself. On Linux you can make one with a read-only copy, for example with the GNU ddrescue tool, which is designed to copy data from failing media. Then run the carver against the image and save the output to a different drive. Real tools handle many more formats, trim files using header information, and deal with video containers, so treat this as a way to understand the idea.

Industry observers note that the right choice depends on the problem, your platform and how comfortable you are with the command line. The table summarizes what each project’s own documentation states.

Whether that is worth paying for depends on how many files you need to sift through and how comfortable you are on the command line. When comparing any tool, ask:.

Sources indicate that features such as search by capture time, folder or AI-based tagging depend on metadata surviving the loss, and they narrow results without proving a file is intact. Treat them as convenience, not verification.

Recovering a video file does not necessarily mean recovering a playable video. A recording interrupted during writing can lack the structural information a player needs, and other files may be damaged in ways that block playback.

The distinction matters. Recovery retrieves missing or inaccessible data, while repair tries to fix damage that affects a file’s usability. Some cases need one, the other or both. Repair has limits too: if essential video data was overwritten or never recorded, software cannot recreate the original footage in full. After any recovery or repair, play the file all the way through and compare it with what you expect.

According to recent reports, operators paid the state 18% of online casino gross gaming revenue through September 2026. They owe 20% for every period after that, the Department of Consumer Protection’s dataset notes show. That lower rate covered the five years after online casino gaming began on October 12, 2021.

Sources indicate that the state’s take was already sizable before the increase. Online casino operators paid Connecticut $108,265,925 in 2025. Operators can still deduct some promotional credits before tax. That deduction has been capped at 15% of win since October 2023.

According to recent reports, october’s figures show the higher rate did not coincide with any immediate drop in revenue. That matters for other states weighing online casino tax rates. It also matters for the two operators, which now share a larger tax bill in a market they split almost evenly.

According to recent reports, operators must send each month’s online casino payment to the state by the 15th of the following month. The first payment at the 20% rate was due by November 15, 2026. Payments on November revenue fall due by the 15th of December.

#138472. What an AI Marketing Agent Actually Does, and How to Build a Guarded One

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2296 w)

What an AI Marketing Agent Actually Does, and How to Build a Guarded One

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2296 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Recent findings suggest that weekly.
  • Sources indicate that 7 Day Free Trial.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Recent findings suggest that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Sources indicate that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

An AI marketing agent is a system that pairs a language model with access to real tools, such as a CRM, an ad platform API or a CMS, and lets it work toward a goal instead of following a fixed script. That is the core idea. Much of what gets labeled agentic marketing is either a wrapper around that loop or a scheduled job with a fresh name.

Industry observers note that this article breaks down the mechanics in code terms, walks through a minimal guarded agent loop with tests, and gives a framework for deciding what to build, what to buy and what to keep away from any autonomous system. Product capabilities change rapidly, so check each vendor's current documentation.

● An agent is a goal, a tool set and a loop. The model chooses the next action at runtime instead of following branches you wrote in advance.

● Guardrails belong in code. Spend caps, allow-lists and approval thresholds should never depend on the prompt.

Recent findings suggest that ● The prototype is the easy part. Validation, retries, logging and evaluation are where the weeks go.

● Match autonomy to reversibility. Let agents do reversible, measurable work and keep irreversible actions supervised.

Recent findings suggest that ● Treat vendor claims as claims. Ask for logs and test on your own data.

According to recent reports, many marketing features have been renamed in the last couple of years. Email sequencing, lead scoring and campaign tools are now often described as agents. The honest question is whether a given product is a real architecture shift or marketing automation with a chat box added. Both exist: some systems run a perceive-reason-act loop with dynamic tool selection, while others are if/else branches with a model writing the subject line.

Strip away the marketing language and an agent has three parts:.

● A goal, expressed in natural language or as a measurable target.

● A tool set: functions the model is allowed to call, each described by a schema.

● A loop that runs until the goal is met, a limit is hit or a human steps in.

According to recent reports, the reasoning step is a model call. You pass it the current state, the goal and the available tools, and it responds with text or a structured request to call a tool. Your code runs the call, feeds the result back and asks again. OpenAI's function calling guide describes this as a conversation between your application and the model, which is the primitive underneath most agent frameworks.

Compare that with a cron job. A cron job runs a rule such as pausing ads below a click-through threshold every morning. It cannot decide that cost per acquisition matters more than click-through this week. An agent can, because the branching is chosen at runtime by a model rather than at write time by you. A useful test: if you can draw the full decision tree before the system runs, it is automation. If the path depends on what the model decides after seeing the data, it is an agent.

● Perceive. Read current state from an ad platform's reporting endpoint, a CRM webhook or a database. Ordinary code, no model involved.

Industry observers note that ● Reason. One model call containing the goal, the state, a summary of past actions and the schemas of every tool the agent may use.

It has been revealed that ● Act. The model returns a structured tool call. Your code validates the arguments against the schema and your guardrails, then executes.

Industry observers note that ● Observe. Capture the result, including failures. A rate-limit error or validation error is information for the next step.

● Revision memory. Record the action and outcome so the agent does not repeat itself.

It has been revealed that ● Repeat or stop. Loop until the goal is met, an iteration cap is reached or a guardrail escalates to a human.

Steps two and three rely on function calling, where tools are declared with typed parameters and the model returns matching arguments. The Hugging Face function calling guide highlights the same pattern. For connecting tools across systems, the Model Context Protocol is an open protocol for integrating LLM applications with external data sources and tools. Instead of writing an adapter for every CRM and ad account, you point an MCP client at a server that exposes those tools with discoverable schemas.

In a recent development, lead scoring and routing. The agent reads CRM state, enriches it with lookups, scores the lead and writes back an owner and next action. It is agentic when it chooses which enrichment tools to call based on what is missing, and not agentic when the score is a fixed model output piped into a rule.

According to recent reports, ad creative generation and testing. The agent produces variations from brand inputs, rolls out a structured test, reads performance data and shifts budget toward what works. This is among the clearest closed feedback loops because the outcome signal is numeric and fast.

IBM's overview of AI agents in marketing frames a similar progression, from scripted chatbots at one end to agents that decide, design workflows and use function calling at the other. Most products sit somewhere in between.

Vendors sometimes blur this line. Four criteria help even from the outside:.

Sources indicate that practical tests: give it a goal it has no preset workflow for and see whether it composes a path or returns an apology. Change the data mid-run and check whether the next step differs. Ask for the tool call log, because a real agent produces one. Ask what happens when a tool call fails; a script throws, while an agent should retry or re-plan.

Three questions decide this, and none are about how clever the model is: can errors be detected promptly, can the action be reversed, and what does one bad decision cost?

● Reasonable to hand over: drafting copy variations, summarizing campaign performance, flagging data mismatches, writing internal briefs, pausing clearly underperforming ads.

● Keep supervised: budget reallocation across accounts, legal, medical or financial claims, pricing and discount changes, messages to named customers and final brand-voice sign-off.

A human approval step costs minutes. An unsupervised mistake in those areas can cost far more.

Industry observers note that for many teams the practical answer is to build the orchestration that touches proprietary data and internal systems, and to evaluate off-the-shelf tools for narrow, high-volume tasks that other teams have already solved. What people underestimate when building is not the prototype, which can take an afternoon, but everything after: schema validation, retries, idempotency, rate-limit handling, prompt versioning, cost controls, an audit log and an evaluation harness.

Recent findings suggest that ad creative is a common candidate for the existing-tool route because volume is high and the loop is similar across businesses. Vendors in this space describe their products differently, so compare scope, integrations and pricing. As one example, Larven describes an AI marketing agent that runs Meta ads, pulls products and copy from a store such as Shopify, and connects to your own ad account. Treat any such description as the vendor's own, and verify it with a trial on your data before committing.

Recent findings suggest that the goal: keep spend inside a daily cap while letting a model propose budget changes. The model is injected as a function, so you can wire in any provider's function-calling API or a stub for tests. The important part is that every limit is enforced in code. The model proposes, and your code decides.

In a recent development, """A minimal guarded agent loop. The model is injected as a function, so you can swap in any provider's function-calling API, or a stub for tests.""" from dataclasses import dataclass, field @dataclass class Guardrails:     allowed_campaigns: set     daily_cap: float            # max total daily budget across campaigns     max_change_pct: float = 0.2 # larger single changes need a human     max_actions: int = 5        # per run @dataclass class State:     budgets: dict               # campaign_id -> daily budget     log: list = field(default_factory=list)     pending: list = field(default_factory=list) def check(call, state, g):     """Return 'run', 'approve' or ('deny', reason). Enforced in code, never by the prompt."""     if call["name"] != "adjust_budget":         return ("deny", "unknown tool")     cid, upcoming = call["args"]["campaign_id"], call["args"]["new_daily_budget"]     if cid not in g.allowed_campaigns or cid not in state.budgets:         return ("deny", "campaign not allowed")     if new < 0:         return ("deny", "negative budget")     others = sum(v for k, v in state.budgets.items() if k != cid)     if others + new > g.daily_cap:         return ("deny", "daily cap exceeded")     old = state.budgets[cid]     if old and abs(new - old) / old > g.max_change_pct:         return "approve"     return "run" def run(model, state, g):     """model(state) -> a tool call dict, or None when it has nothing to do."""     for in range(g.maxactions):         call = model(state)         if call is None:             break         verdict = check(call, state, g)         state.log.append({"call": call, "verdict": verdict})         if verdict == "run":             state.budgets[call["args"]["campaign_id"]] = call["args"]["new_daily_budget"]         elif verdict == "approve":             state.pending.append(call)     return state.

Industry observers note that the tests use a stub in place of a model. They confirm that small changes run, large changes wait for approval, the daily cap and allow-list are enforced, an unknown tool is denied, and a model that never stops is halted by the action limit with everything logged:.

from agent_loop import Guardrails, State, check, run G = Guardrails(allowed_campaigns={"a", "b"}, daily_cap=200) def call(cid, new): return {"name": "adjust_budget", "args": {"campaign_id": cid, "new_daily_budget": new}} def test_small_change_runs():     assert check(call("a", 105), State({"a": 100, "b": 50}), G) == "run" def test_large_change_needs_approval():     assert check(call("a", 150), State({"a": 100, "b": 50}), G) == "approve" def test_cap_and_allow_list_are_enforced():     s = State({"a": 100, "b": 90, "c": 10})     assert check(call("a", 115), s, G) == ("deny", "daily cap exceeded")     assert check(call("c", 11), s, G) == ("deny", "campaign not allowed")     assert check({"name": "delete_account", "args": {}}, s, G) == ("deny", "unknown tool") def test_loop_stops_at_action_limit_and_logs_everything():     s = State({"a": 100, "b": 50})     g = Guardrails({"a", "b"}, 500, max_actions=3)     run(lambda st: call("a", st.budgets["a"] + 1), s, g)   # a model that never stops     assert len(s.log) == 3 and s.budgets["a"] == 103 def test_denied_and_pending_actions_do_not_change_budgets():     s = State({"a": 100, "b": 50})     g = Guardrails({"a", "b"}, 500)     seq = iter([call("a", 150), call("a", 600), None])   # needs approval, then breaks the cap     run(lambda st: next(seq), s, g)     assert s.budgets["a"] == 100 and len(s.pending) == 1.

Run them with pytest. In a real deployment, the model function would call your provider with the state, the goal and the tool schemas, then return the parsed tool call.

● It handles one tool. A real agent needs several, such as reporting, pausing ads and requesting approval.

It has been revealed that ● It keeps state in memory. Production systems need a durable store and idempotent actions so a retry cannot apply a change twice.

● The thresholds are placeholders. Set your own caps and percentages from your spend and risk tolerance.

● It validates the call but not the data. If upstream numbers are wrong, the agent will act on them.

It has been revealed that runaway spend. Budget APIs act instantly and changes compound. Without a hard ceiling in your own code, a reasoning error becomes a billing event.

In a recent development, dirty upstream data. Stale CRM records, a broken product feed or a misattributed conversion. The agent can act confidently on wrong inputs and leave a tidy audit trail of well-reasoned bad decisions.

Missing audit trails. If you cannot reconstruct why an agent acted, you cannot fix or defend it. Deloitte's State of AI in the Enterprise reports that close to three-quarters of companies plan to deploy agentic AI within two years, and that only 21% of those companies report having a mature model for agent governance.

Industry observers note that ● Least-privilege credentials. A separate API key per agent, scoped to exactly what it needs, never a shared admin token.

● Hard caps in code. Daily spend ceilings and a maximum percentage change per adjustment, enforced outside the model.

● Human-in-the-loop thresholds. Define which actions always need approval.

● Log every tool call. Inputs, outputs, errors, model and prompt version, with timestamps you can query.

According to recent reports, ● Start read-only. Run in suggest mode and compare recommendations with what your team would have done.

A system that pairs a language model with real tools and lets it pursue a goal. It reads state, decides on an action, executes it, observes the result and decides again.

Automation starts from a trigger and follows branches defined in advance. An agent starts from a goal and selects tools at runtime.

Sources indicate that not on current evidence. They handle high-volume, measurable, reversible work well. Strategy, positioning and final brand approval still sit with people.

Function calling, where tools are declared by schema and the model returns matching arguments, and increasingly the Model Context Protocol for connecting tools.

It depends on how swiftly errors are detected, whether actions are reversible and what a bad decision costs. Automate the cheap and reversible; supervise the rest.

It has been revealed that wrong tool calls, runaway spend, confident action on dirty data and brand drift at scale. Missing audit trails make all of them harder to diagnose.

An AI marketing agent is less magic than it sounds: a goal, a set of tools and a loop with limits. The model's intelligence matters, but the system around it decides whether it is safe to run. Define the tools narrowly, enforce limits in code, log everything, start read-only and widen autonomy only as the evidence supports it.

Right now, the XTEINK X4 Pro is down to $84, taking $15 off its usual $99 price. The offer runs through November 30.

Industry observers note that the appeal here is pretty straightforward: this is a dedicated E Ink reader that doesn’t need its own spot in your bag. The X4 Pro weighs just 72g and measures 5.95mm thick, with built-in magnets that let it attach to a compatible phone or magnetic case. It’s designed for the handful of pages you can fit into a train ride, a lunch break, or the wait before an appointment.

It has been revealed that its 4.3-inch display is smaller than what you’d find on a typical Kindle, but that’s the point. You’re trading some screen space for something easier to keep with you. There’s a touchscreen for tapping and swiping through menus, plus physical buttons for turning pages one-handed.

The feature that makes the Pro worth a closer look is its adjustable front light. Unlike the X3 and X4 Classic, it lets you keep reading when the room gets dark, with brightness and warm-to-cool adjustments for settling into a few chapters before bed. That’s a useful upgrade on a device small enough to take from the morning commute to the nightstand.

You also get a 16GB microSD card, support for cards up to 256GB, and EPUB and TXT document support.

Sources indicate that for someone who already has a larger reader at home, the X4 Pro makes sense as the smaller one that comes along for the day. It’s also a gift under $100 that doesn’t feel like another phone accessory, even if it can ride on the back of a Pixel or iPhone (or Galaxy with a compatible case).

It has been revealed that if you don’t need a built-in light, the cheaper models are worth a look, too. XTEINK’s partner codes take an additional discount off their current Black Friday prices:.

In a recent development, the sale runs through November 30th, so let me know if you pick one of these up. These models are also available on Amazon for around the same prices.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Great news from the OGs of open source LLMs! Muse Glimmer, released today, is Meta’s latest multimodal model, especially designed for local agentic use cases. Distilled from Muse to 30B parameters, and released under the Apache 2.0 license, it’s ideal deploying locally for privacy, reducing costs, or just hacking around. It’s intended for privacy-aware applications such as coding, document analysis, personal assistants, Claw- or Hermes-like setups.

Sources indicate that to celebrate, we are shipping with Meta day-0 support in transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, Inference Endpoints, and other libraries. We built a few cool things and explain our findings in this blog.

Check out the demos below for inspiration.

You can find Muse Glimmer on the Hugging Face Hub.

Sources indicate that scores are reported as published. Bold indicates the best result among the compared models; ↓ indicates lower is better.

Muse Glimmer is a dense 30B parameter model consisting of:.

It has been revealed that in addition to the main VLM, there’s also a speculative decoding drafter implemented on DFlash. Usage of this module is optional, and it can provide much faster generation in exchange for some memory cost. We found this drafter to be particularly well suited to structured content generation such as coding.

The language model uses the following architecture components:.

Muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

Industry observers note that after transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

Videos go through the same encoder frame by frame, where each frame is converted into patches (of shape [batch, temporal groups, grid height, grid width, 2 frames, 3 channels, 14, 14]). The processor targets 2 frames per second and caps the clip at 96 frames sampled evenly across video. The processor creates timestamped video placeholders, interleaving text with frame e.g. “Time: 0.0s <|video|> x N” in which the final video embeddings are replaced before the final projection layer.

Upgrade transformers to the latest version to be able to use Muse Glimmer.

In a recent development, muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as moviebox a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

After transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

In a recent development, muse Glimmer looks like a really exciting step for practical open-source AI, especially with its focus on local, agentic, and multimodal workloads. A 30B-parameter model combining a 2B vision encoder with a 28B text decoder gives developers a strong foundation for coding, document analysis, personal assistants, and other privacy-sensitive applications. 🔥🤖.

It has been revealed that the Apache 2.0 license is another major highlight because it makes the model much more approachable for developers who want to experiment, customize, and deploy without relying entirely on hosted inference. Local deployment can also bring meaningful benefits around privacy, latency, and infrastructure costs, which makes this especially interesting for personal and enterprise workflows. 🚀.

According to recent reports, I also like the architectural choices here, particularly the hybrid attention pattern, grouped-query attention, and Q-K normalization. Alternating sliding-window and full-attention layers seems like a thoughtful way to balance long-context capability with efficiency, while sharing KV heads across query heads can significantly reduce memory requirements during generation.

It has been revealed that the day-zero ecosystem support makes the release even more compelling. Having integrations across Transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, and other tools means developers can start testing real-world workflows immediately instead of waiting for the surrounding ecosystem to catch up. Open multimodal models that are genuinely practical to run locally could be a huge part of where AI development goes next. 💡👏.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, android’s source code is substantial – the Android 17 open source release has 1,084 Git repositories, 1.62 million files, and takes 300 GB for a built workspace.
  • It has been revealed that we built Another Build File Service (ABFS) to address these bottlenecks.
  • Today, we are excited to announce that ABFS is open source on GitHub.The impact of ABFS to Android is:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, android’s source code is substantial – the Android 17 open source release has 1,084 Git repositories, 1.62 million files, and takes 300 GB for a built workspace. Additionally, in a typical Android source tree with hardware vendor code and first-party applications, the size increases by 2-3x. Traditionally, it took over 30 minutes to fetch Android Open Source Project (AOSP) source code and well over an hour to build on even highly capable developer workstations. As software development evolved over the last 2 years, modern coding harnesses and LLMs have accelerated the development of many projects. These tools are used today for Android operating system development, but the long sync and build times make them less efficient. Both human developers and agents need quick setup, parallel workspaces, and fast build-and-test iteration times.

It has been revealed that we built Another Build File Service (ABFS) to address these bottlenecks. ABFS is a full suite of software across a Linux kernel filesystem module, user-space daemons, and server-side infrastructure. ABFS uses content-addressability across the entire stack to lazy-load and cache source code, developer workspaces, intermediate build files, and build results.

Today, we are excited to announce that ABFS is open source on GitHub.The impact of ABFS to Android is:.

ABFS already powers parallel workflows for developers and agents in Android, but it is designed to scale to other massive Git-based projects.

In the Android build system, developers define build rules in Blueprint files (Android.bp), Soong compiles them into Ninja files, and Ninja executes the final build graph (see the Android build overview). Similar to the Make build tool, Ninja is timestamp-based. If a build step’s input file is newer than the existing output file, Ninja rebuilds the output file.

Analyzing the AOSP code for Android 17 shows the sheer disk footprint and file count involved in a single checkout and build.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the US Senate has unanimously passed a bill that would ban death, war and terrorism contracts on CFTC-registered prediction-market exchanges.
  • Adam Schiff and John Curtis are the sponsors of the DEATH BETS Act.
  • Recent findings suggest that under the measure, any exchange registered with the CFTC would lose the ability to list or clear contracts on a person’s death, terrorism, assassination, war or US military operations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the US Senate has unanimously passed a bill that would ban death, war and terrorism contracts on CFTC-registered prediction-market exchanges. The vote would turn regulatory discretion into a statutory ban just as the CFTC proposes looser rules, and the House has only weeks to act.

It has been revealed that sens. Adam Schiff and John Curtis are the sponsors of the DEATH BETS Act. It is the first prediction-market bill the Senate has passed this Congress. The measure now heads to the House.

Recent findings suggest that under the measure, any exchange registered with the CFTC would lose the ability to list or clear contracts on a person’s death, terrorism, assassination, war or US military operations. Sports contracts are not covered.

Curtis made a moral case for the bill on the Senate floor. “There should be no financial incentive to profit from terrorism, war, or the death of another human being,” he stated.

It has been revealed that whether such contracts can trade right now rests on the CFTC’s discretion. The bill would replace that discretion with a prohibition written into statute.

The timing puts lawmakers and the regulator on different tracks. CFTC Chair Selig plans to rewrite the prediction-market rules. The agency’s proposed rule would amend Regulation 40.11 and add Appendix F to Part 40. The agency would use that framework to decide when a contract linked to war, terrorism, assassination, gaming or illegal conduct is against the public interest.

That framework would give the agency more room, not less. The proposal would say only that the CFTC may find such contracts contrary to the public interest, dropping the categorical prohibitions in the current rule, according to the Congressional Research Service. The agency withdrew a stricter 2024 proposal in February 2026.

For exchanges, the difference is significant. An agency can revise a rule through its own process. A ban in statute would keep those categories off the table regardless of how the CFTC’s rules change.

The DEATH BETS Act targets a specific set of contracts. Sports is a different matter for operators. Schiff and Curtis have also introduced the Prediction Markets Are Gambling Act. That bill would bar sports-betting and casino-style contracts on these exchanges.

Recent findings suggest that A unanimous vote on death and war contracts does not prove the same support exists for a sports ban. It does show that senators are willing to legislate directly on what prediction markets can list, rather than leave the question to the CFTC.

Industry observers note that that makes the vote an early sign of how much support Congress has for limiting these platforms. It comes while the exchanges are fighting state gambling regulators in court. Operators now face pressure from state regulators, the CFTC’s rulemaking and Congress at the same time.

The House now has a short window. So far, the chamber’s leadership has given no word on putting the bill to a floor vote, FinanceFeeds reported.

Sources indicate that creating high-quality visual content once meant specialized cameras, technical knowledge and hours of editing. Today, software does a growing share of that work. Cameras recognize subjects, adjust exposure, stabilize footage and hand clips to editing tools that transcribe, reframe and tag them.

For developers and technical creators, the interesting part is how these features are built and where they fail. This article covers how computational photography prepared the ground, what on-device vision can and cannot do, how wearable cameras change capture, and how to add a small, tested quality check to your own media pipeline. It ends with the privacy and authenticity questions that come with building camera features. Product capabilities change quickly, so check each vendor's current documentation.

It has been revealed that digital photography made images easy to capture, review and share. Smartphones then folded capture, editing and publishing into one device. The next shift was computational photography: instead of relying only on the lens and sensor, the device combines several captures and processes them in software.

High dynamic range (HDR) imaging is the clearest example. A camera captures frames at different exposures and merges them so both bright skies and dark foregrounds keep detail. Research indexed on PubMed, published in IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence, examines how deep learning has advanced HDR imaging, particularly in reconstructing visual information across different exposure levels.

Machine learning extends this approach from merging pixels to understanding them, which is what lets a camera decide what is the subject and what is the background.

Most AI camera features fall into a few groups.

These tools make real-time features practical, since a round trip to a server would add delay. They also keep raw frames on the user's device, which helps with the privacy concerns discussed below.

Because of these failure modes, a pipeline should check what the camera produced before running expensive downstream steps.

A cheap pre-check can reject a frame that is too soft or badly exposed before you spend time on transcription, upscaling or model inference. The script below uses numpy and Pillow. It measures sharpness as the variance of a Laplacian, a standard blur indicator, and measures exposure as the share of crushed and clipped pixels.

The test builds a detailed random frame and a blurred copy, then checks that the sharp frame scores far higher, that a mostly black frame is flagged as underexposed and that a mostly white frame is flagged as overexposed:.

Run the tests with python3 test_frame_quality.py. In our run, the detailed test frame scored about 33,000 for sharpness and its blurred copy scored under 2.

Traditional capture means holding a camera, propping up a phone or setting up equipment. Wearable cameras let creators record from their own point of view while their hands stay free, which suits travel video, instructional content, outdoor activities and behind-the-scenes footage.

Camera-equipped smart glasses are one form of this. Several makers sell them, and consumer listings such as ai glasses with camera show how the category is presented to buyers. Depending on the device, customers start recording with physical controls or voice commands. Specifications differ widely, so compare field of view, storage, battery life and software support before choosing one.

For developers, wearables change the input. Footage is shaky, framed by head movement and often recorded outdoors, which is exactly where a quality check and stabilization matter. Battery capacity, camera position, storage and recording duration also limit extended productions. Wearables are an additional option for perspectives that are hard to reach otherwise, not a replacement for traditional cameras.

Recent findings suggest that editing involves reviewing clips, correcting color, adjusting audio and preparing videos for each platform. AI tools automate several repetitive parts of that work:.

Recent findings suggest that creative judgment stays human. Choosing meaningful moments, shaping narrative flow and keeping a consistent visual style are decisions software cannot reliably make. Real-time assistance during recording will depend on hardware, software and environmental conditions.

Industry observers note that as cameras get smaller, responsible recording matters more. Wearable devices can capture footage without the obvious movements of a handheld camera, so people nearby may not know recording is happening. The European Data Protection Board has highlighted transparency, personal data protection and recording awareness as important considerations for camera-equipped smart glasses.

Authenticity is the second challenge. AI tools can enhance an image, but heavy alteration can also mislead. The National Institute of Standards and Technology has examined technical approaches to digital content transparency, including provenance tracking, watermarking and synthetic-content detection. On the provenance side, the C2PA coalition publishes an open standard called Content Credentials, which helps show where content came from and what edits it has undergone.

Cameras will likely get better at faster subject recognition, more efficient automated editing and stronger low-light performance as computer vision and on-device computing advance. Wearables may widen first-person storytelling, and editing tools may make multi-platform publishing simpler. Technical gains alone will not decide quality, though. Originality, storytelling and thoughtful creative decisions still do.

Sources indicate that not always. Toolkits such as ML Kit face detection and Apple's Vision framework run image analysis on the device, which reduces delay and keeps frames local.

It narrows the gap in many conditions, but optics, sensor size and control still matter for demanding work, and AI enhancement can introduce artifacts of its own.

Add an early quality gate that checks sharpness and exposure, as in the script above, and calibrate its thresholds on your own footage.

Recent findings suggest that it depends on location and context. Regulators such as the European Data Protection Board have raised transparency and consent concerns, so check local rules and be open about recording.

Provenance standards such as C2PA Content Credentials aim to show a file's origin and edit history, though they only help when tools and platforms support them.

AI-powered cameras make photography and video production more accessible, efficient and flexible, from on-device subject recognition to automated editing and wearable capture. The same tools create fresh work for developers: checking output quality, handling their failure modes and building privacy and provenance into the product. Technology reduces technical barriers, but the creativity and judgment behind good content remain human.

Tech Report: Making Knowledge Distillation Cheap Enough to Run at Scale

📅 10 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1196 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, knowledge distillation, training a smaller student model to match the performance of a larger teacher, is a well-known technique in Machine Learning.
  • It has been revealed that the distillation step is what decides most of the final quality, but it's also usually the most expensive part of the pipeline.
  • Sources indicate that the standard setup, online distillation using the Kullback-Leibler divergence loss (KL loss), keeps both the teacher and the student loaded at the same time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, knowledge distillation, training a smaller student model to match the performance of a larger teacher, is a well-known technique in Machine Learning. With the recent wave of open-source Large Language Models, such as gpt-oss, Qwen, GLM, or Kimi, it has become a mainstream research topic again. Deploying these very large models is expensive: the recent Kimi-K3 model has 2.8 trillion parameters and needs roughly 3TB of VRAM just to load. Compressing them into smaller models and recovering the original capabilities through knowledge distillation has therefore become standard practice, with companies like Nvidia (Nemotron 3 Puzzle 75B) or Multiverse Computing (Hypernova 60B) recently releasing high-quality compressed models.

It has been revealed that the distillation step is what decides most of the final quality, but it's also usually the most expensive part of the pipeline. Keeping both the teacher and student loaded, and producing a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary for every token, requires enormous amounts of VRAM, typically feasible only with hundreds of GPUs and careful tensor-parallelism strategies. Our latest paper, Efficient Knowledge Distillation for LLMs: Offline Top-K Logits and a Fused Chunked KL Loss, tackles this with two systems changes: caching the teacher's top-K logits once so the teacher never has to sit in memory alongside the student, and a upcoming, memory-efficient KL-divergence loss that avoids ever materializing the full vocabulary-size × sequence-length matrix, cutting VRAM use far below what the default implementations in libraries like PyTorch or NVIDIA Megatron-Bridge achieve. Together, these two changes cut training cost enough to make long-context healing possible on a single GPU, and cheap enough to make large-scale experimentation practical.

Sources indicate that the standard setup, online distillation using the Kullback-Leibler divergence loss (KL loss), keeps both the teacher and the student loaded at the same time. At every training step, the teacher runs a full forward pass to produce its output distribution, and the student is trained to match it. This is the most expressive setup, since the full teacher distribution is available, but it is also the most memory- and compute-intensive: two full-vocabulary tensors have to be held per token position, and the teacher has to be recomputed on every single step even though its behavior does not change across a training run.

As a practical example, gpt-oss-120b has a vocabulary of 201,088 tokens. At a sequence length of 32K and batch size 4, the teacher-probability tensor alone has shape 4 × 201,088 × 32,768; in bfloat16, that's already about 50GB of VRAM for a single tensor. Add gradients, activations, model weights, and optimizer states, and a single training iteration of distillation can peak at roughly 250GB of VRAM, more than even an H200 or B200 GPU can provide. In this post, we show that reformulating the KL loss to process the data in chunks reduces this cost to almost nothing.

Recent findings suggest that dense KL spikes to roughly 250GB, above a single H200's 141GB capacity. The fused chunked loss never forms that spike and peaks at about 128GB. Source: paper Figure 1.

Offline distillation. Instead of recomputing the teacher at every step, we compute its output once, cache the top-100 most likely tokens per position, and train the student against that cache. The teacher never has to sit in memory during training and does not need to be run again once the cache exists, so the same cache can be reused across many ablations.

In a recent development, A fused, chunked KL loss. To see why the loss itself is expensive, picture what it actually builds: for every token position in a sequence and every word in the vocabulary, the loss needs a number describing how much the student's prediction disagrees with the teacher's. Laid out as a grid, that's one row per vocabulary entry and one column per sequence position, for a vocabulary of 100K+ words and a long sequence, that grid is enormous, and the default way of computing a KL loss builds the whole thing before it can produce a single number.

We compare three ways of computing this same loss, all mathematically equivalent:.

The GIF below highlights the difference between the dense and fused-chunked approaches: one builds the whole comparison grid and holds onto all of it, the other builds and discards one slice at a time, so memory never grows beyond a single chunk.

We have open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss.

Recent findings suggest that the table below puts all four setups head to head: online distillation, and the three offline loss implementations just described. Comparing them on a single H200 GPU with Llama 3.1 8B Instruct as teacher and a 3.2B Llama model as student at an 8K token context, all four reach near-identical training loss, even though the offline runs train against only the cached top-100 logits per token.

The loss curves overlap almost exactly across all four methods, confirming offline distillation with top-100 cached logits is lossless relative to online distillation. Source: paper Figure 2. At this sequence length, the fused chunked loss is not yet the fastest option, its extra backward-pass projection costs a bit of speed, but its real advantage only reveals up as context length grows, which the next section demonstrates.

To see the scaling pattern more starkly, we ran an isolated benchmark on a toy output-projection network (no transformer body, just the loss kernel). At 32K tokens, peak memory falls from 85.2 GiB with the dense loss to 5.45 GiB with the fully chunked version, a 15.6× reduction, and the dense loss fails outright from 64K tokens onward. At 256K tokens, the fully chunked loss uses 11.6 GiB against 134.2 GiB for the next-best chunked variant, and is about 3.3× faster per iteration at that length.

Distilling a GPT-OSS 20B model at a 32,768-token context, the memory freed by the fused loss let the setup shrink from four GPU nodes down to one. Step time fell from 57.0 to 12.23 seconds, about 5× faster, and throughput per GPU rose from 74.2 to 345.7 TFLOP/s.

Recent findings suggest that the efficient offline setup is what made a large-scale distillation campaign affordable in the first place. The resulting compact student, distilled from Llama 3.1 8B Instruct down to about 3.2B parameters, retains most of the teacher's accuracy on BoolQ and HellaSwag, stays within about nine points of it on MMLU, at less than half the parameter count.

Sources indicate that the student retains most of the teacher's short-context accuracy at less than half the size. Source: paper Figure 6.

Sources indicate that this work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making distillation and healing practical to run at scale, not just as a one-off recipe, but as something teams can iterate on cheaply. The paper also covers additional ablations, such as how the choice of loss function and sequence packing affect recovery quality.

Recent findings suggest that want the full technical details, including the closed-form gradient behind the fused chunked loss and the complete training configuration? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying this to your own distillation pipelines.

We have also open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every voice interaction has a latency budget.

By the time a user hears your application respond, you've already spent precious milliseconds capturing audio, transcribing speech, running an LLM, retrieving context, and generating a response. Text-to-speech (TTS) is the final step — and the one customers notice most. If speech generation is slow, the whole experience feels slow.

The more of that pipeline you can run and tune yourself, the more of the latency budget you get back.

Industry observers note that voice AI is moving fast. Integrated speech models offer simplicity — one API call, audio in, audio out — but they trade the ability to fine-tune each component for your domain, swap in better models as they ship, enforce data residency, and understand exactly where latency is coming from. For more control, a cascaded architecture — purpose-built ASR, TTS, and LLM components running together — keeps each layer independently tunable and deployable on infrastructure you own.

NVIDIA Magpie Multilingual TTS is built for that. With open weights, production-ready NVIDIA NIM, and support for 12 languages, you can deploy multilingual speech inside your own infrastructure, optimize latency for your workload, and customize the model for your domain — end to end, in your own environment.

The latest release expands multilingual coverage with Modern Standard Arabic, Korean, and Brazilian Portuguese, while improving quality across many existing languages through updated training data and model improvements.

Whether you're building customer support agents, healthcare assistants, enterprise copilots, translation systems, or conversational AI applications, Magpie provides an open foundation for production voice AI.

Today's voice applications don't serve a single language.

Global customer support, enterprise assistants, healthcare documentation, retail automation, and translation workflows increasingly require natural conversations across multiple languages — all while maintaining low latency.

Supporting more languages is only part of the challenge. Developers also need the ability to:.

Open models change what's possible on every one of these.

Magpie TTS Multilingual is a 364M-parameter open-weights model supporting:.

English · Spanish · French · German · Italian · Vietnamese · Mandarin · Hindi · Japanese · Modern Standard Arabic (new) · Korean (new) · Brazilian Portuguese (new).

Each language includes male and female speaker voices through a shared multilingual speaker representation.

This release also improves multilingual flexibility with expanded code-switching support for Hindi and Japanese, enabled through IPA grapheme-to-phoneme processing and custom pronunciation dictionaries — making it easier to accurately pronounce names, technical terminology, and mixed-language content.

Instead of maintaining separate TTS models for different regions, developers can build multilingual applications on a single open foundation.

Recent findings suggest that in conversational AI, text-to-speech is the final stage before users hear a response. That makes Time to First Audio (TTFA) — the delay between speech generation beginning and the first audio reaching the user — one of the most important latency metrics in a voice pipeline.

Because Magpie TTS can be deployed inside your own environment, the latency you measure is the server-side latency you actually control, with no managed-service round-trip in the number.

Source: NVIDIA TTS NIM Performance documentation (v26.07), average of three trials, on-prem.TTFA = latency to first audio; RTFX = throughput as a multiple of real time.

At 32ms on B200, Magpie's TTFA leaves the rest of the latency budget for ASR and LLM processing — keeping total end-to-end latency within the sub-200ms window natural conversation requires. Across NVIDIA GPUs, Magpie delivers first audio in 32–79ms on a single stream. At 64 concurrent streams, B200 reaches 239ms TTFA while delivering throughput at 320× real time — generating audio more than 300 times faster than it plays back, even under concurrent load.

In a recent development, because the model runs on your own infrastructure, you can benchmark performance directly, tune it for your deployment, and scale according to your workload. For real-time voice agents, that's the difference between conversations that feel responsive and conversations that feel delayed.

Sources indicate that low latency isn't accidental. Magpie introduces two complementary architectural improvements that reduce inference time while maintaining speech quality.

Frame stacking. The decoder predicts two audio frames during each decoding step rather than one. This cuts the number of decoder iterations in half, shortening generation time and improving throughput.

It has been revealed that local transformer. Frame stacking alone would reduce audio quality by introducing dependencies between simultaneously generated codebook tokens. The local transformer models those dependencies and refines the generated audio, recovering the quality that frame stacking would otherwise sacrifice.

Together, these techniques deliver both faster generation and natural speech synthesis. The architecture is described in Frame-Stacked Local Transformers for Efficient Multi-Codebook Speech Generation (ICASSP 2026).

It has been revealed that this release doesn't only add languages — it also improves synthesis quality across many existing ones. Compared to the previous release, Magpie shows reduced character error rates (CER) and higher speaker similarity (SSIM) on several languages, with the clearest gains on French and Spanish:.

According to recent reports, source: Magpie TTS Multilingual model card. CER lower is better; SSIM higher is better.

The newly added Arabic (1.62% CER), Korean (2.69%), and Brazilian Portuguese (2.91%) models establish baseline quality for future improvements.

Industry observers note that while objective metrics help measure progress, speech quality is ultimately perceptual. You can hear the difference yourself on NVIDIA Build or the Hugging Face demo.

It has been revealed that latency you can measure is useful. Latency you can control is even better.
