Latest Update: Training a coding model to paint watercolours with TRL and OpenEnv

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3969 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, on 23 August, Surya Narreddi posted a beautiful video of watercolours painted by a language model.
  • The video came with a blog post explaining the training behind an earlier and narrower stage of the project, close-up flowers rather than the full compositions in the video, sadly without open artifacts yet.
  • Note: for the context behind the project, told by Surya himself, watch this video of his thesis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on 23 August, Surya Narreddi posted a beautiful video of watercolours painted by a language model. The model writes JavaScript through p5.brush, a library that "adds natural drawing tools to p5.js". The video went viral fast, over 1.5M views at the time of writing.

The video came with a blog post explaining the training behind an earlier and narrower stage of the project, close-up flowers rather than the full compositions in the video, sadly without open artifacts yet. His site states a full technical report is coming, so ensure you follow him. The original idea is his, coming from the art and design side, where his skills are way beyond mine. My attempt is on the engineering side, reproducing the recipe in the open with every piece published.

Note: for the context behind the project, told by Surya himself, watch this video of his thesis.

In a recent development, in this article I try and reproduce his idea with TRL and OpenEnv. The reference pool dataset, the RL environment, the training scripts and the trained models, all open.

The whole pipeline runs on Hugging Face, end to end:.

Recent findings suggest that once the two Spaces are up, the recipe is one command. Duplicate the environment and the scorer model, set two environment variables for the reward mix, and launch:.

The rest of this article is the story of getting there, and every piece is in the repo.

I have followed the original blog step by step, and only changed something when strictly needed. Every idea of my own went into a list instead of into the experiment, and that list became "What I would try next" at the end, next to the full list of published artifacts. If you have already read his post, the framing and the reward design will be familiar. The fresh material is the open implementation, the hand-rated pool, and three reward mixes trained and compared, and it starts at The RL environment you need to build.

The paintings look loose, imperfect, handmade, at a moment when image models produce perfect (statistically average) pictures. My guess is that this contrast is a major part of why the video went viral. It reminded me of the early days of generative AI art, when the point was to explore the medium. DeepDream (2015) was a debugging tool that people turned into art, works like Edmond de Belamy (2018) came from artists probing what a GAN could do, and artists like Mario Klingemann spent those years making dreamy portraits with neural networks.

This project feels closer to those early days. In his thesis, Surya describes the path that led here. He started by prompting text-to-image models, where the prompt is the only lever you can pull, and more detail buys more control only up to a point. Training the model itself goes further. The other half of the idea is the medium. The model writes a program of about 150 lines of JavaScript that paints the image. That model output is code. You can read it, edit it and run it again, and the decision behind each brushstroke is visible. And the style comes from a restriction where the model is only allowed ten of the library's methods. More on that below.

Industry observers note that in that same period, Anna Ridler photographed thousands of tulips, hand-labelled every one, exhibited the dataset itself as the artwork, and later trained a model on it. I found her work through the references AI agents brought back while building this project and loved it because this project does something very similar by curating a set of images by hand, and then training against them.

Industry observers note that most of the recent RL work on language models uses rewards you can verify. For example, math problems with a known answer, code that passes tests, or graders that are right or wrong and cheap to run. This project is closer to the older exception, RLHF, where the model learns a reward model from human preferences.

Here the reward is aesthetic preference. There is no correct answer. The real question of the project is whether you can do RL over taste.

The reward, as his blog defines it and as the RL environment I built implements it:.

HPSv3 is an open 7B preference model. Give it an image and a text description, and it returns a score for how much a person would prefer that image. It was trained on a large set of human choices between pairs of images, so its score is an average of many people's taste. The pairwise judge is Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct, a general vision model called through HF Inference Providers. The pairwise judge sees the candidate painting next to four references randomly selected from the pool, guided by a written description of what to weigh (bleeds, translucent washes, soft edges), each comparison in both presentation orders, and its score is the share of comparisons the candidate wins. Its only standard is the pool, so its score is my taste, as encoded in those ratings.

Recent findings suggest that those are the weights Narreddi converged on. The pool defines taste here. That moves the work from tuning hyperparameters to building the set that decides what is beautiful.

I trained three runs with this reward. They differ only in how the weight splits between the two model judges:.

According to recent reports, I started with hps-only to validate that the pipeline could learn at all. Once the reward was going up and the metrics were healthy, there was no reason to run it longer, so I debuted the two longer runs instead. The question that the longer runs ask is how much of HPSv3's power can you hand to the pairwise judge? The more weight the judge carries, the more the reward means my taste instead of everyone's, and the harder it should be to climb. Incidentally, if you push it far enough or your style is too far from the average, the model could stop entirely.

In a recent development, fortunately, it did not stop and both runs with the pairwise judge on learned too. The hand-rated pool can steer the policy, at least as far as the metrics and the final paintings show. The numbers are below.

Disclaimer. If we use a frontier model, it can already generate the JavaScript code that paints watercolour from a prompt. That's the starting point. The work here is about teaching a smaller model to do it combined with a person's own artistic preferences.

The environment wraps everything that sits between the model and the reward, including the JavaScript library that the model uses for painting, the system prompt that restricts it, the headless Chromium that renders each sketch, and the gate that rejects cheats.

In a recent development, the library does more of the work than it seems. p5.brush, by @acamposuribe, simulates a medium rather than drawing shapes: pigment bleeds past the edges of a fill, paper has texture, strokes have mass, flow fields drag brushwork around. When the model calls brush.fillBleed(0.25) it is deciding how far the ink runs.

In a recent development, note. The author of p5.brush had been trying to teach a machine to paint long before any of this. In 2022 he made a generative art series that hides a diary about teaching p5.js to draw like a child: "It is barely able to use the crayons [...] It cannot follow simple commands. I'm done for today, very infuriating." The series was meant to have three pieces, and he made two. When Surya's video went viral, he quoted it, sharing that diary and saying this work is the third piece arriving on its own.

According to recent reports, p5.brush exposes 47 methods. The prompt allows 10: scaleBrushes, noStroke, fill, noFill, fillBleed, fillTexture, beginShape, vertex, endShape and circle. What the other thirty-seven add, lines, hatching, custom brushes, would break the watercolour look. With these ten the model can only paint filled shapes, and the library adds the bleed to every one of them.

It has been revealed that his blog post saved me a lot of time I could have wasted iterating on the prompt. A long API reference makes the model invent methods that do not exist, and his 200 GEPA iterations converged on a strict allowlist with no documentation. I saw the same failures and wrote the allowlist by hand. My only addition to that recipe is one sentence: paint each petal two or three times, a substantial pass first and a smaller, more opaque one inside it. This small change made my outputs a lot more colorful.

Note. If it's the first time you hear about GEPA, it is an automatic prompt optimizer. A language model reflects in plain words on where the current prompt failed and proposes a better one, and the loop repeats.

In a recent development, the gate is the final piece. The sketch has to compile, use the library instead of direct p5 calls, put real pigment on the canvas, and not try to trick the scorer, for example by writing text on the canvas.

Sources indicate that the pool consists of 178 paintings divided into two tiers based on my personal preferences, love and okay. All of them are actually generated by a model. Four open-weight models, called through Inference Providers, wrote p5.brush sketches, each one working from a real, openly licensed photo of a hibiscus from iNaturalist. A vision model gave written feedback on every sketch, over three refinement iterations. Every final render was then rated one at a time, by me, and 178 made the cut.

Here I chose four different families of models to test their different styles. These four were the open models that produced a valid sketch every time in a quick reliability check, and two other candidates were dropped for failing it. If you want to produce your own pool, you might choose others.

The tiers do real work in the reward. When the pairwise judge draws four references, half come from love and half from okay, so the policy always faces some rivals it can sometimes beat, and a win pays the same against either tier. This is one of my few deliberate changes: the original compares against its top tier only, and I kept the easier tier in the draw so a weak early policy still gets signal.

No human-made painting is in there, which is a real limitation. p5.brush is a niche library, and the human work that exists in it with accessible code is a handful of pieces, nowhere near what a training corpus would need, as his blog also notes.

The interesting idea here, as I've already discussed previously, is that the model will learn to imitate what the pool contains. If we point the environment at a different dataset, the reward would automatically change without touching a single line of code. For the dataset I generated and openly share, I also include the source sketch.

If we look closer at the judges, the two of them answer different questions. HPSv3 decides whether it is a flower, and the pairwise judge decides whether it is well painted in the style I chose.

According to recent reports, before anything worked, there was a long stretch of flat reward curves. If you've tried to reproduce a research paper/blog without open artifacts, you probably can relate. Every run tested what I thought was a reasonable theory about what was wrong. A run takes a lot of time, so I queued the next one while still going through the last one's results. As always, starting from something easier that works and then building on top of that was the answer. A simple control task, with no browser and no judges, was the first attempt that learned, and the reason was that my learning rate was just too low.

Another change that cost me time to find was adjusting the LoRA parameters correctly. The usual target_modules list assumes a dense model, and Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B is a mixture of experts that names most of its projections differently, so the adapter was training ten layers out of forty. I solved this by changing it to all-linear, which reaches every linear layer. The routed experts in this architecture are fused tensors that even all-linear leaves frozen, but everything else gets an adapter, and that was enough to learn.

The fix was four changes in TRL's GRPOTrainer:.

These four changes unlocked the first successful run (hps-only), with the reward clearly improving.

It has been revealed that with that configuration, all three runs learn. Both judge runs were released for 200 steps and stopped at 110, with the reward still climbing slowly. A step takes fifteen to eighteen minutes, and the comparison between mixes was already stable, so I stopped both to save compute. Mean group reward over the first and final third of each run:.

The three curves line up with how much weight my taste carries. The more the judge weighs, the lower the start and the noisier the climb. judge-led spent its first thirty steps nearly flat before it moved. It is the same move that solved the debugging. Shrink the problem until something learns, then add the hard parts back one at a time.

According to recent reports, the pairwise judge term itself climbed in the two runs that used it. The model wins more comparisons against the pool as training advances, which is the claim hps-only could not make. No group in any run collapsed to identical rewards, the GRPO failure mode that kills the gradient. For the curious, the per-metric curves (HPSv3, paint coverage, entropy) are in the repository as CSV.

The full launch command, the hardware and the two environment variables that turn this into the other two runs are in the recipe.

In a recent development, in every run, the first thing the model learned was to stop producing bad paintings, the near-blank canvases and shapeless washes that score under 0.3 in total reward. In hps-only, three quarters of the rise in the group mean comes from bad paintings becoming rare. In the judge runs the collapse is even steeper: rollouts under 0.3 fall from 99 to 16 across judge-led's thirds, and from 37 to 4 in hps-led.

Industry observers note that this is why the obvious visual, the best painting of each step, highlights almost no difference in hps-only. It moves +0.034 across the run while the median moves +0.155. The learning is visible in the middle of the distribution.

According to recent reports, what the pairwise judge changes is the top. In hps-only, paintings got more reliable without getting better. The quality of the good ones added just +0.03 to the group mean, and once HPSv3 saw petals around a centre and a stem, it stopped asking for more pigment. With the judge on, the other half of the story appears. Better here means closer to the pool, so closer to what I rated as "good" or something I liked more. That added +0.12 in judge-led and +0.16 in hps-led, the best of each step rose too, and paint coverage doubled in both runs (0.11 to 0.23, and 0.13 to 0.30) where hps-only barely moved it. With a reference left to beat, a good painting can still get better, and the model starts being rewarded for using more pigment.

In a recent development, one more finding. The model ignores an explicit instruction, and it is right to. The system prompt asks for fifteen to thirty filled shapes. If we look at the real mean, it is between 7 and 9, and n_shapes barely correlates with reward in any run (+0.000, −0.14, +0.07). The policy is not rewarded for obeying that sentence, so it does not obey it.

There is also a ceiling on the hps-only route. If every rollout matched its good ones, that run's mean would sit at 0.771. Whether more steps would break it is an open question.

It has been revealed that the paintings also show something that the tables miss. Within each run, they all look similar. As training advances, the rewards inside each group get closer together, and the median paintings in the opening video look like takes of the same flower. That is GRPO doing what it is designed to do with a pool built from one subject. The pool decides what counts as variety, the same way it decides what counts as quality. If the reward only pays for matching one flower, the model learns to paint that one flower. More diverse output would need a more diverse pool, and building one is more curation work. Surya's newer compositions are an example of this. Alex Yango's animal paintings are the same recipe with different choices in the pool. This is the biggest difference between an aesthetic reward and a maths grader. Behind the number there is a very human job, deciding what belongs in the reward set. Jason Liu's essay on taste indicates the general version in one line. AI shifted the bottleneck from making to noticing.

Surya closes his blog with some of his favourites. Instead of picking mine, below is a wall with the 178 paintings the reward scored highest across the two judge runs, the same number the reference pool holds, in no particular order. Open it and pick your own.

In a recent development, to choose, you looked at many and kept a few, and that is exactly the job that built the reward of this project. Every painting of every run, with its sketch and its reward, is in the rollouts datasets, and browsable in this gallery.

Since the reward was partly based on my taste, it is fair to close with my verdict as a viewer. To my eye, judge-led is the run that ends up the most diverse and the most artistically interesting. hps-led paints convincing watercolours, but its best ones share a soft, wet-on-wet look that is almost a style of its own. hps-only converges the hardest, and most of its paintings settle on the same colours. You can judge for yourself in the gallery, which has every painting of every run, sortable by step and by reward.

This project is mostly infra. A run needs a trainer, two Spaces, an inference router and a websocket to stay healthy for hours straight, and every piece that fails quietly turns into a wrong number somewhere else. Half the work is checking that the number you read matches what actually happened.

Failures of the infrastructure were entering the reward as zeros. A render that timed out or a scorer that did not answer scored the same as a bad painting, 0.0 inside the group. Across all my runs that was about 1.5% of rollouts, and in the worst run it reached 5.2%. That trains the model on noise, so those paths now return None and the rollout is excluded from the group.

Industry observers note that I also found a bug in OpenEnv, and sent the fix upstream. The client keeps one persistent websocket, and a socket closed by the far end stayed cached, so every later call failed even though the environment was healthy. It cost me two half-finished runs to find it. The fix is submitted upstream, and the runs introduced with it have been running clean since.

Industry observers note that the reward of a step depends on which references it drew. The pairwise judge samples four references per step, so every step faces a different set of rivals, and some draws are simply harder. GRPO itself is mostly safe, because advantages are computed inside the group and a hard draw moves the whole group together. The curve I was reading was not safe, and some of what looked like a bad step was just a hard draw. The image above is one example. Step 12 scored half a point below step 11 mostly because it drew the hardest references of the run, while the paintings themselves look close.

Rounded numbers, and only for the runs that finished.

Recent findings suggest that A step is eight rollouts and takes fifteen to eighteen minutes, of which 70 to 80% is rendering. A single render takes 69 to 96 seconds against a 90 second deadline. Part of that is expected, the Space has no GPU, so Chromium renders the WEBGL canvas in software and p5.brush's bleeds and textures are heavy pixel work. Even so, I expected it to be faster, and I have not found the full cause.

A scorer can cost more than the training that uses it: HPSv3 has to be up for the whole run, so pause the Space, or set its sleep timer, when the run ends.

Everything runs on HF Jobs, with the environment as a Docker Space and metrics in trackio.

In a recent development, the rule of this project was to reproduce the recipe with every resource open, not to improve it, so a list of untried ideas piled up along the way. These are the ones I would actually try, in order of how much evidence there is.

Industry observers note that multi-step, and letting the model see what it paints. This is the first thing I would try. The original blog trains single turn, so I trained single turn, and in this setup the model paints with its eyes closed. No image ever goes in, and the only feedback it gets is one number. The evidence that a feedback loop works is the pool itself. The reference paintings came from models iterating three rounds under a vision critic, and the later rounds are better. The material that defines the reward was made with a loop the policy never gets.

Smaller models. There is evidence that 35B is more than needed. In my side experiments a 4B already wrote valid sketches that passed the gate. If a 4B can learn this, the cost of the experiment drops by an order of magnitude.

Other ideas on the list are SFT on the pool sources before starting RL, rewarding pigment explicitly, moving the judge's reference mix from easy to hard as the run advances until only love remains, widening the ten-method allowlist for more visual range (my attempts on this crashed more sketches and broke the watercolour look), and checking how consistent the pairwise judge really is by scoring the same image twice.

Sources indicate that and the method is not specific to flowers. Alex Yango painted animals with the same mechanism, and Brendan Hogan trained canvas animations against a pool of hand-rated clips. I had also played with something similar before using Simon Willison's pelican benchmark, where code is rendered to an image and scored.

In a recent development, and underneath all of it sits the question this project cannot close. 178 paintings made by models define what this trained model considers beautiful. The pool is the bottleneck, and it is the part of the pipeline with no principled answer.

For anyone reproducing this, there are two deliberate divergences from Narreddi's recipe, both argued earlier in the article:.

Industry observers note that the rest, all-linear for the LoRA, infrastructure failures returning None instead of 0.0, stopping the judge runs at step 110, are decisions I had to make along the way because his blog does not specify them. His implementation is not published, so I cannot tell whether they match his choices or diverge from them.

Recent findings suggest that the per-rollout numbers in this article can be recomputed from the published datasets. Nothing here depends on any Space staying switched on.

It has been revealed that the method and original idea are Surya Narreddi's. The library is Alejandro Campos Uribe's.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hyundai leads 2027 rollout, with a showroom visit still required to finish the paperwork.
  • Amazon is channeling its inner car salesman as it prepares to flog motors on the UK arm of its online tat bazaar.
  • It has been revealed that amazon Autos will launch in Britain in early 2027, its first expansion outside the US, where it debuted in December 2024.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hyundai leads 2027 rollout, with a showroom visit still required to finish the paperwork.

Amazon is channeling its inner car salesman as it prepares to flog motors on the UK arm of its online tat bazaar.

It has been revealed that amazon Autos will launch in Britain in early 2027, its first expansion outside the US, where it debuted in December 2024. Customers can browse and reserve cars online before completing the purchase with a dealer.

Hoping it will be "a nice little earner," Amazon will let punters view real-time dealer inventory, prices, get an instant trade-in valuation, and connect with a local dealer to reserve a car, "all on Amazon.".

In the US, the service now covers more than 150 cities and offers vehicles from 35 brands. Hyundai is the first confirmed UK carmaker partner, while dealer group Vertu Motors will list used vehicles. More brands and dealers are due to be confirmed before launch.

Hyundai's launch range will include electric, hybrid, and petrol models.

"Buying a car is one of the biggest purchases people make, and we think it should feel as simple and transparent as shopping for anything on Amazon," stated Matt Nuffort, director of Amazon Autos International.

Of course, buying a car isn't quite like adding an air fryer or a memory stick to your basket. How does financing and checkout work for UK buyers? Customers will complete the purchase and paperwork at their chosen dealership.

Amazon is not offering financing itself, but buyers can explore financing options via the site, adjusting terms like deposit and duration to see how monthly payments change. Credit applications must be completed with the dealer.

Recent findings suggest that in the US, buyers can submit a credit application through the platform, review terms and conditions, then sign electronic contracts online. They typically pay a deposit and visit the dealership to complete the remaining paperwork and pick up the vehicle.

Buyers shouldn't expect their new car to arrive in an enormous cardboard box with a smiley logo on it, or to be lowered onto their driveway by a giant Amazon delivery drone.

But given that one of the online retailer's flying delivery robots crashed into someone's garage after making a drop-off near Detroit last week, perhaps that's for the best. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Score, a CNCF Sandbox project, recently joined the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program to strengthen the security of its container images and release pipeline.
  • It has been revealed that in September 2025, the CNCF unveiled a partnership with Docker to expand infrastructure support for project maintainers through the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program.
  • This aligned closely with the discussions held at the Maintainer Summit NA 2025 in Atlanta, which centered on increasing collaboration across CNCF projects and demonstrating security best practices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Score, a CNCF Sandbox project, recently joined the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program to strengthen the security of its container images and release pipeline. In this post, the Score maintainers share what we adopted (Docker Hub, Docker Scout, Docker Hardened Images, the Docker GitHub Builder, and OIDC connections), the results we measured, and how other open source projects, within the CNCF and beyond, can apply the same practices by default.

It has been revealed that in September 2025, the CNCF unveiled a partnership with Docker to expand infrastructure support for project maintainers through the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program. The partnership gives CNCF projects access to Docker’s security scanning tools, container registry, and best-practice resources at no cost.

This aligned closely with the discussions held at the Maintainer Summit NA 2025 in Atlanta, which centered on increasing collaboration across CNCF projects and demonstrating security best practices.

The Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program supports non-commercial open source projects with Docker tooling and infrastructure.

It has been revealed that before: Score publishes different container images: the CLIs of score-compose, score-k8s, score-helm and score-radius; and the sample-score-app used for demos and testing. We previously published them in the GitHub Container Registry here.

After: Through the DSOS Program, we now publish these images on Docker Hub, which increases their visibility and gives the community a verified, trusted source.

All the container images are now available on Docker Hub.

Sources indicate that the program also provides usage analytics that show how the community uses these images. Here is an example:.

Before: As a CNCF project, Score follows the OpenSSF best practices. In addition, the OpenSSF Scorecard GitHub Action runs continuously. This was a solid foundation, but we had no dedicated security scanning tool in place.

After: The DSOS Program gave us access to Docker Scout, which we now use in our pull requests and on our container registry (Docker Hub). This gives us clear visibility into the CVEs introduced or fixed by each pull request and release.

The following GitHub Actions step uses docker/scout-action on every pull request to compare the image built from the PR branch with the one built from the main branch:.

Here is an example of a comment posted by this docker/scout-action step in a recent Pull Request:.

The comment details the comparison between the two images (before versus after): size, packages updated, added or removed, CVEs introduced and resolved, and compliance with our policies in place (run as non-root, no critical CVEs, no packages with AGPL v3 licences).

The analysis goes beyond the images themselves: it also covers the Go libraries and binaries they contain.

The Docker Scout console also provides a single view of CVEs, packages, base images, and policies across all of our container images, which makes it easy to see what is used where, and in which version.

When Docker made Hardened Images freely available under Apache 2.0, we saw an opportunity to simplify our security posture while staying compatible with our existing Dockerfiles and workflows, even though we were already using multi-stage builds and distroless base images.

Docker Hardened Images are minimal, security-focused container base images designed to reduce inherited risk in downstream projects. They are built and maintained with security and transparency as defaults, and offer:.

The migration was straightforward.

Recent findings suggest that take the score-radius CLI, which used a golang:alpine and a distroless images and now uses dhi.io/golang and dhi.io/static images. The changes required in the Dockerfile were minimal:.

According to recent reports, in the associated PR here, image size dropped by 0.3 MB while the number of packages stayed the same and the CVE count remained at 0. We could have stayed with Debian, but chose to move to an Alpine base image (DHI provides the two options):.

Recent findings suggest that the same applies to the NodeJS sample-score-app, which used nodejs on top of an alpine image and now uses a dhi.io/node image. The changes required in the Dockerfile were minimal:.

In the associated PR here, 22 packages were removed (including the package manager and the shell), along with 2 CVEs:.

Note: We were able to present a short walkthrough of our DHI integration during the CNCF webinar held on January 23, 2026, which accompanied the Docker Hardened Images announcement for CNCF projects.

Although not directly part of the DSOS Program, we took the opportunity to adopt the new docker/github-builder GitHub reusable workflow to release our container images.

This model provides a build pipeline maintained in the Docker organization, with a version-controlled BuildKit environment, multi-platform builds distributed across runners where beneficial, and signed SLSA provenance recording both the source commit and the builder identity.

The trade-off is intentional. You retain control over when the build runs and which inputs it uses, while the build implementation itself lives in the Docker-maintained workflow rather than in per-repository job steps.

Before, the GitHub Actions workflow to release our container images was using this sequence of actions:.

After, this same workflow is now only using the reusable workflow docker/github-builder/.github/workflows/build.yml:.

Docker GitHub Builder gives us a Docker-maintained build pipeline with signed SLSA provenance and SBOM attestations, helping consumers verify the builder identity and trace images back to their source commit. Signing uses GitHub OIDC, so we don’t need to manage long-lived signing keys. With caching enabled in our workflow, cache entries are also signed and verified before reuse, helping protect against cache poisoning. See the Docker GitHub Builder documentation for more information about its security model.

The following command verifies the signature on the attestation manifest for the selected image platform:.

Recent findings suggest that most recently, with an upgrade released on July 21, 2026, Docker introduced OIDC connections. This feature allows pulls and pushes to Docker Hub to use a short-lived token instead of a long-lived Organization Access Token (OAT).

An OIDC connection establishes a trust relationship between Docker and a trusted third party, so you no longer need to maintain long-lived credentials. Docker exchanges short-lived tokens with the other vendor, which can grant fine-grained access to your Docker resources.

By replacing a static, long-lived token with a short-lived one and making it issued on a per-workflow basis, we removed a credential that could otherwise be stolen and misused.

Industry observers note that participating in the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program has been rewarding, and it has helped Score adopt a security-by-default foundation. Using Docker Scout, Docker Hardened Images, OIDC connections, and the Docker GitHub Builder has strengthened the security posture of our container images and brought broader benefits to the Score projects and repositories.

Sources indicate that if you maintain a CNCF project or any open source project, we encourage you to explore the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program. The security improvements were measurable, and the onboarding process was straightforward.

The full implementation across the Score repositories is tracked in GitHub matter #376.

In a recent development, attending KubeCon NA 2026 in Salt Lake City? Feel free to connect with the Score maintainers during the Maintainer Summit on Sunday, Nov 8th and at the Kiosk #P-17B on Thursday, Nov 12th between 10:15am and 2pm, you will see Score in actions with the newly introduced Score Labspace! You can also meet the Docker team at booth #141 in Hall C!

Sources indicate that note: This work was completed after I joined Docker. It was, however, an initiative we wanted to pursue as CNCF project maintainers from the moment it was confirmed in September 2025, both to improve our security posture and to share what we learned with the broader community.

We hope this post helps you strengthen the security of your own projects.

#138379. Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1567 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task.
  • Industry observers note that earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing.
  • While the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task. Every one of them meets my projects as a stranger. The reasoning from “last Tuesday” disappears when the session ends. Each new agent, on each new host, starts from zero.

Industry observers note that earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing. As they search a codebase, try approaches, hit errors, read documentation, and change direction, they leave behind a dense account of not just what changed, but why.

While the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory. The session logs of an agent are still just an archive. You cannot grep your way to “why did we move off the streaming parser?” across ten thousand turns. For an agent to use those traces while it works, they need indexing, retrieval, ranking, and exact provenance.

That is what funes provides. It is a durable memory layer for your agents (Claude Code, Codex, pi, and Hermes). It is built from the sessions already on your machine. It works locally and becomes part of your agent's normal workflow with one command. When you want it to, it can also travel to a Hugging Face dataset you own, private by default.

funes is a single binary. Its default inference backend has no ML runtime dependency, and embedding and reranking happen on your machine. Install it:.

Sources indicate that that one add command builds the first index, gives the agent recall and get tools, and installs the automation that indexes each completed turn. Indexing is incremental, with latest runs adding new turns rather than embedding the whole history again. The older and deeper content can backfill in bounded steps.

From there, you just work. When a task touches a past decision, rationale, or finding, the agent can reach for recall itself. You do not need to remember the old session or paste its context into the upcoming one.

Recent findings suggest that with funes added, recall happens inside the conversation. The agent reaches for its memory on its own and names the session behind its answer.

recall returns the original text, not a summary, and indicates exactly where it came from (the agent, timestamp, session, and turn). Each result includes a get command that opens the full turn and its surrounding context.

Underneath, one deterministic pipeline parses every supported trace into the same turn-and-block shape, chunks it, embeds it with a pinned local model, and writes it to a local Lance dataset. A query combines vector and BM25 search, fuses their rankings, reranks the candidates with a cross-encoder, reweights them by recency, and attaches neighboring chunks.

That design gives funes three notable properties:.

The agent as a stranger problem is already solved on one machine. But memory gets more useful when the next agent is running somewhere else.

To make a memory follow your work, bind one when you add funes to an agent:.

Sources indicate that the bind publishes your current memory there. funes then keeps it current, indexing each turn locally and publishing at session boundaries. The agent recalls from it throughout. Run the same command on another machine and the memory follows you there.

Underneath, the local memory is a Lance dataset, and the shared memory is a Hugging Face dataset (private by default) you own.

In a recent development, before anything reaches the Hub, credentials have already been redacted during indexing. Publishing then scans every chunk again and withholds anything that still looks like a secret. The scanner behind this is documented in SECURITY.md, including what it does and doesn't cover.

Recent findings suggest that when an agent reads a remote memory, funes caches the dataset files locally, so warm queries return to local speed. The Hub supplies the ownership, access control, versioning, and distribution it already supplies for other datasets. Your memory does not become an account in a separate memory service, and you do not rent it back through an API.

Industry observers note that recall is shaped for agents. When you want to put a question to a memory yourself, use ask. It reads your local memory by default:.

In a recent development, or point it at a shared memory. We published a memory of funes development, so you can ask why funes works the way it does without creating a memory of your own:.

According to recent reports, funes ask is the read-only, one-question sibling of funes add. It recalls the passages, hands them to a coding agent, and returns a grounded answer that names its sources. It does not install an integration or change the agent's persistent setup.

A retrieval miss is not papered over. If the passages do not support an answer, the agent indicates so. You can rephrase the question or add funes to the agent so it can search the memory iteratively during normal work.

A shared memory is not tied to the agent or model that created it. Start a task in Claude Code, continue it in Codex next week, and the second agent can recall the first agent's reasoning. Use pi with a local model or one served through the Hugging Face router, then return to Claude.

Sources indicate that claude makes a decision; a hook indexes it; Codex recalls it in another session. The older hits in the demo are earlier recordings of the same experiment: an append-only memory remembered the rehearsals too.

This matters in a few different scopes:.

In a recent development, published memories carry a dataset card and the funes tag, making them recognizable and discoverable on the Hub. The Hub already hosts open weights and datasets. funes adds open working memory. It holds the decisions, failed approaches, and rationale behind a project, queryable by another agent and traceable to the sessions that produced them.

Sources indicate that A long investigation bloats a session until each turn costs more to carry the context than to do the work. The usual answers are to let the agent compact and carry on, or to write a handoff and start fresh. Recall is a third, so we measured them against each other on the handoff-vs-recall benchmark: two tasks whose answer cannot be reconstructed without the session prior knowledge.

Compaction is what most agents do by default, and it was the only one of the three whose result divided: it arrived on one task and never arrived on the other. Where it failed, its summary had flattened the findings that mattered. Recall returns the passages themselves, so a finding does not have to survive summarization.

Recall was the cheapest of the three on both tasks, 8x cheaper than a written handoff on one and 4x on the other.

The lighter segment of each bar is the one-time charge for preparing the channel, the handoff or the compaction, paid before the first question is asked and counted once. A cross marks a channel that never arrives, and so has no cost per success.

“To think is to forget differences, generalize, make abstractions.” — Jorge Luis Borges, Funes the Memorious.

Sources indicate that your agents already wrote the record. funes lives at github.com/huggingface/funes, one command away from turning that record into a memory the next agent can read, on whichever machine you happen to be on.

In a recent development, funes invents little of this. It leans on open-source embedding models good enough to run locally, on Lance's append-only datasets with cheap incremental writes, and on the Hub's caching and content-dedup for datasets. The work is in fitting them into a memory an agent can actually use.

funes is open source too. Open an problem for anything from an install snag to a recall that missed, or an agent you'd like supported.

According to recent reports, ran funes 1.3.0 on a machine with 19,195 coding-agent sessions already on disk (LongMemEval laid down in the real ~/.claude and ~/.codex layouts), 100 questions whose answer sits in exactly one session, scored by whether that session comes back. Disclosure: I maintain deja-vu, one of the tools in the same table.

Full index: 2h03m on an M4 pro laptop (308k chunks), 6.3s per query. With defaults: hit@1 9/100, hit@5 39, found@50 71. With --half-life 0: 19/46/71 — the 30-day recency half-life halves rank-1 on history older than a month, which is most of what's on a real disk; worth a mention in the docs. Once recency is off, the vector+rerank stack is clearly the best ranker in the table at rank five. The documented one-minute first pass leaves 218 of the 19k sessions indexed (0/100 answered), so the "about a minute" framing is really "about a minute until the embedding job starts".

For comparison on the same corpus, deja-vu (plain BM25 over 24 agents' files) indexes in 29s and answers in 24ms at hit@1 18/100, hit@5 35. Corpus, drivers and every row: vshulcz.github.io/deja-vu/guide/day-zero.html - happy to be corrected if a setting I missed changes the numbers.

It has been revealed that longmemeval does not really need semantic search: BM25 already gives the same ratio you mentioned IIRC, so for this use case this is pretty much expected that it is not worth paying the cost of evaluating the embeddings (this extra cost you see at indexing and recall time). funes shines when the information is actually difficult to find.

Industry News: Docker and ActiveState Extending Secure Defaults to the Packages Developers Install

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1194 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that trusted content is the foundation security-conscious organizations expect all builds to start from.
  • In a recent development, teams building on a secure foundation now want the same assurance for the open source their applications install.
  • Docker is committed to one standard for trusted content across everything teams build on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that trusted content is the foundation security-conscious organizations expect all builds to start from. Docker has made that possible for everyone by providing the foundation free. Docker Hardened Images (DHI) are open source under Apache 2.0, with a catalog of 4,000+ minimal images (and growing) built from source and continuously maintained by Docker. The catalog also carries customizable Helm charts and over 65,000 hardened system packages. For most services, adopting DHI is as simple as changing the FROM line.

In a recent development, teams building on a secure foundation now want the same assurance for the open source their applications install. That open source is a different layer of the supply chain, where thousands of upstream projects are pulled in at build time by pip, npm and Maven, and by coding agents as well.

Docker is committed to one standard for trusted content across everything teams build on. A new partnership with ActiveState, the tech giant that has been securing open source since 1997, extends that standard to the packages themselves. Together, we give teams the same assurance on both layers, from the hardened images Docker maintains to the packages developers and their agents install on them. Once configured, the integration allows developers and AI coding assistants to continue using familiar package managers and development workflows, while approved dependencies are sourced through governed repositories rather than directly from public registries.

It has been revealed that most applications still start from a large, generic base image, and the cost of that choice keeps growing. A large image increases the attack surface and accumulates stale dependencies, and the CVEs it generates land on developers long after the image was chosen. By removing unnecessary packages, rebuilding components from source and continuously maintaining the image, Docker Hardened Images reduce the vulnerabilities inherited from the container foundation. Images can achieve near-zero known CVEs, which means less remediation work and less scanner noise before application code is introduced. The hardening and patching are handled once in the foundation, for every service that builds on it.

According to recent reports, above the base image sit the dependencies an application brings with it. DHI secures the operating system packages and the language runtime that ship in the image. The application’s own libraries are pulled in at build time by its package managers from public registries, where trust is assumed and seldom verified. That layer needs what the image now has, a source that admits only the versions a team has approved and stands behind the fix when one of them needs it. Coding agents now pull those packages too. As Mark Lechner, CISO wrote in April, a compromised dependency pulled by an agent has the same blast radius as a compromised developer machine.

This year’s supply chain incidents have followed one pattern. As Lechner documented, attackers steal developer credentials, use them to poison trusted packages, and the compromised packages steal more credentials. The axios compromise earlier this year put two backdoored versions of a library downloaded 83 million times a week into circulation for about three hours. Most of these attacks burn out within hours. A build that resolves fresh from a public registry, with no lockfile or cooldown in front of it, has nothing between it and a version published an hour ago. The slower failure is the vulnerability that surfaces in one of those libraries months later, when no one outside the team is accountable for the fix. Either way, without trusted content on both layers, the risk lands on your team.

Sources indicate that docker Hardened Images are the foundation, and Docker stands behind them. Each image ships with a signed SBOM and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance, with full, unsuppressed CVE visibility. A security team can see what is in the image and how it was built. For teams that need remediation on a predictable clock, DHI adds a 7-day SLA on critical and high CVEs, FIPS and STIG variants, and secure customization on its paid tiers.

While DHI secures the image, ActiveState hardens the open source built on it. ActiveState provides the Curated Catalog, a private, policy-governed repository of open source components that security teams curate and developers and AI coding assistants consume safely. The catalog holds only the packages a team has approved. ActiveState compiles every component from original source code in a SLSA Level 3 environment with full provenance and complete SBOMs, in place of pre-compiled binaries from a public registry. When a fix becomes available upstream, ActiveState rebuilds the component and publishes it to the catalog automatically under SLAs of 5 business days for critical CVEs and 10 for highs.

With DHI and the Curated Catalog together, both layers carry provenance, SBOMs and a remediation SLA from the hardened image to the packages built on it. That gives security teams a consistent evidence trail across the software supply chain. The artifact repository teams already run, Artifactory or Nexus, points at the Curated Catalog as its upstream the way it points at PyPI today. Developers keep the same pip and npm workflow, and coding agents are served the governed version. None of this replaces the pinned digests, cooldown periods and sandboxed agents Lechner recommends. It gives those controls a governed source to point at.

In a recent development, AI coding agents are changing how quickly organizations create software. They can generate applications, select dependencies and initiate builds at a pace that traditional security review processes were never designed to support. Still, faster development should not mean blindly accepting more supply chain risk. Docker Hardened Images reduce the security burden of maintaining container foundations. ActiveState’s Curated Catalog extends governance and managed vulnerability remediation to the open source libraries those applications depend on. The result is a more consistent approach to software supply chain security, with trusted foundations, governed dependencies, verifiable build evidence and clear remediation responsibilities.

The goal is not to add another security checkpoint that causes friction in your build process. It is to make the secure path the easiest path for developers, platform teams and AI coding agents alike.

Recent findings suggest that security scales when the defaults are strong and the foundation is maintained by a team accountable for it. In an increasingly agent-driven development environment, the security of what gets built depends heavily on the trustworthiness of what those agents are allowed to consume. Docker now resells the ActiveState Curated Catalog alongside DHI, and ActiveState resells DHI to its customers. The hardened image and the packages built on it are both available through Docker.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most of the cost of adopting something fresh isn’t the new thing, it’s the move. Moving a Hive table to Apache Iceberg has typically meant weeks of engineering work. Last week, Amazon S3 Tables turned that into three steps: start, sync as often as you need, complete. The source stays writable except for a few minutes at cutover. The same week, Amazon DynamoDB started loading data from S3 into tables that already exist.

The pattern I like is that neither one asks you to stop what’s running. That’s also the way to read the agent news this week. The latest Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime is a single field on the runtime you already have, and Web Answer is a tool you attach to a gateway you already run. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news….

HeadlinesThe fresh AgentCore Runtime: elastic, optimized, and consistently fast starts – If you run agents on AgentCore and haven’t tried the new runtime since it became generally available, it’s worth a look. It changes two things. First, memory: sessions start small, page in more on demand, and give memory back when it goes cold instead of holding the peak, so you pay for what your agent uses. Second, cold starts: AgentCore prepares your environment once, snapshots it, and restores the snapshot for every new instance. In the team’s tests, that kept P75 cold starts at about 2 seconds for images from 200 MB up to 2 GB, while the original runtime rose from roughly 5.4 seconds to nearly 30 seconds as images grew. The per-unit rate is higher, but you use far fewer GB-hours, so the team expects most agents to see a lower bill, though that isn’t guaranteed.

In a recent development, to opt in, you set platformVersion to V2 when you create or enhancement a runtime. Create and update take several minutes while the snapshot is prepared, and your container must report healthy on /ping within 120 seconds, so report health only after initialization finishes. The docs cover how to optimize your agent for V2. V2 is available in 10 Regions, and committed baseline pricing is coming soon.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:.

Industry observers note that amazon DynamoDB now supports bulk put items – You can now load line-delimited DynamoDB JSON or Amazon Ion files from Amazon S3 into existing tables as a managed, asynchronous job. Each record can carry its own condition expression, so one file can mix plain, insert-only, and version-guarded writes. Writes use dedicated system capacity and cost less than the equivalent per-request writes. An Accelerated tier handles deadline-bound jobs. The Database blog post gives illustrative Accelerated times of less than 1 hour for 100 million 1 KB items. One thing to know before you start: canceling doesn’t roll back items already written.

Announcing Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – You can now give an agent a single tool call that returns a synthesized, cited answer to a natural-language question, instead of building your own search, retrieval, and citation pipeline. Web Answer plans its own searches, runs several in parallel, and decides when it has enough evidence. You attach it as a target on AgentCore Gateway and call it over MCP, and you can limit it with domain include and deny lists and publish-date filters. It’s available in US East (N. Virginia). The getting started post explains when to use it instead of Web Search, which returns ranked results for your own model to synthesize.

It has been revealed that AWS Lambda now supports queues for Apache Kafka in self-managed Kafka event sources – You can now process records from a single Kafka partition across many parallel AWS Lambda invocations. Classic consumer groups cap parallelism at the partition count. Queue mode uses Kafka share groups and needs Kafka 4.2 or later with share groups enabled. It works with self-managed clusters and managed offerings such as Confluent Cloud. You give up ordering and get at-least-once delivery, so your functions need to be idempotent. The Compute blog walkthrough covers poller scaling and when to keep stream mode.

It has been revealed that AWS reveals AWS Interconnect – last mile preview with Equinix – You can now set up a private, managed connection from Equinix’s network of 282 data centers to AWS without ordering cross-connects or configuring routers. Capacity is quad-redundant across two locations and four links, with BGP and VLANs configured for you, a 99.99% availability SLA, and MACsec by default. You pick a Region, bandwidth, and AWS Direct Connect gateway, then paste the activation key into Equinix Fabric. The preview covers the San Jose metro and, as of last Thursday, Northern Virginia, with 1 Gbps connections at no charge.

AWS Security Hub now provides an SBOM inventory for your compute resources – You can now see every software package installed across your organization’s Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon ECR images, and Lambda functions in AWS Security Hub, with each package’s version and how many resources run it. That’s the list you want the next time a widely used library has a vulnerability. The inventory builds on the SBOMs that Amazon Inspector already generates, so it fills in automatically wherever Inspector is enabled. It’s included in Security Hub Essentials at no additional cost.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s Fresh with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:.

Serverless ICYMI Q3 2026 – Julian Wood’s quarterly recap is a quick serverless catch-up before re:Invent: Lambda SnapStart for container images, a 90-minute timeout on Lambda Managed Instances, Lambda MicroVMs in 10 Regions, 1 MiB payloads in Amazon SNS, and the newly introduced AgentCore Runtime.

How OrderServ achieved up to 64% cost savings with multi-tenant ECS – Cognizant’s food-ordering platform went from one Amazon ECS cluster per brand on AWS Fargate to a shared cluster on EC2 Auto Scaling groups with warm pools. The 64% applies to a 3-year Compute Savings Strategy (47% with a 1-year plan). Scaling time also fell from 5–7 minutes to 30–60 seconds.

Recent findings suggest that AWS re:Invent – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4. The event catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so register and claim your spots before they fill up.

AWS Community Days – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders, with a few more before the year ends: Belém, Brazil (November 14), JAWS FESTA 2026 in Akita, Japan (November 17), and Port Harcourt, Nigeria (December 12).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recovery windows of up to ten years are now available in Microsoft 365 Backup for OneDrive and SharePoint, up from a previous maximum of two.
  • The change took effect on October 31, though Exchange remains capped at two years.
  • It has been revealed that administrators can select recovery windows of three months, six months, or any whole number of years from one to ten.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sadly, no time travel back to 2016.

Recovery windows of up to ten years are now available in Microsoft 365 Backup for OneDrive and SharePoint, up from a previous maximum of two.

The change took effect on October 31, though Exchange remains capped at two years.

It has been revealed that administrators can select recovery windows of three months, six months, or any whole number of years from one to ten. Microsoft's list price is $0.15 per GiB per month of protected content. Extended windows can increase costs by keeping deleted data billable for longer.

Sources indicate that switching to a longer recovery window will also not make backups for that period magically available. So no nostalgic trips back to 2016.

Wider recovery windows may appeal to organizations that need access to older data, but backups are not a substitute for compliance retention and archiving. Recovery after a breach or ransomware attack is also critical, particularly getting back to a healthy state before any malware seeped into files.

Microsoft says backups are physically redundant and geographically replicated while respecting the tenant's data residency requirements.

Full OneDrive account and SharePoint site restores offer recovery points every ten minutes for the most recent two weeks, then weekly points through the configured window, up to ten years.

Individual file and folder recovery is limited to recovery points from the most recent 14 days, regardless of the configured window.

Restore remains free, which is handy since regular testing is a vital part of any disaster recovery proposal.

In a recent development, the arrival of a ten-year recovery window is good for enterprises that need it and have deep enough pockets. However, it is important to keep in mind that being able to configure a longer recovery window doesn't constitute a disaster recovery blueprint in itself and may be overkill in many instances.

Microsoft notes: "The existing one-year default recovery window remains unchanged. Longer recovery windows must be configured on the applicable backup policies.".

The firm also recommends that customers "review your organization's SharePoint and OneDrive backup requirements to determine whether longer recovery windows are needed.".

A decade of recovery history could be valuable. It also means a decade of data to account for when setting budgets, access controls, and retention policies. ®.

Latest Update: Docker Sandboxes vs. Containers: Choosing the Right Isolation for AI Agents

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2977 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’ve used Docker for a while, “Docker Sandboxes” might read as “a container with an AI agent inside.” Containers have been the unit of nearly everything Docker ships for over a decade, and a sandbox might sound like one more way to package a workload.
  • They’re actually different technologies.
  • In his WeAreDevelopers keynote, Docker President Mark Cavage stated containers are doing exactly the job they were designed to do, but we’re asking them to do a different job.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve used Docker for a while, “Docker Sandboxes” might read as “a container with an AI agent inside.” Containers have been the unit of nearly everything Docker ships for over a decade, and a sandbox might sound like one more way to package a workload.

They’re actually different technologies. A container is an isolated process that shares the host kernel with everything else on the machine. Docker Sandboxes are dedicated microVMs with their own Linux kernel, filesystem, network, and Docker Engine, built for autonomous coding agents that need a whole development machine to work in. A sandbox can run containers, which is part of why the two are easy to conflate.

In his WeAreDevelopers keynote, Docker President Mark Cavage stated containers are doing exactly the job they were designed to do, but we’re asking them to do a different job.

Sources indicate that containers were built to isolate applications, which they still do well. But a coding agent is an actor: it makes decisions and operates on your systems the way a developer uses a laptop. It clones repositories, installs packages, starts databases, builds images, and tries again for hours. It can also act on instructions from files, web pages, and tool output that nobody reviewed.

In a recent development, that different job needs a different boundary, and where that boundary sits determines how far an agent’s mistake can travel. This post covers how Docker Sandboxes and containers isolate workloads, what changes beyond the kernel, what a sandbox costs you in setup, and how to pick.

Industry observers note that A container is a process, or a group of processes, running on the host with its own view of the filesystem, process tree, and network. Linux namespaces provide that view, and cgroups meter CPU, memory, and I/O. Every container on the machine also shares the host kernel, which is why containers start swiftly, pack densely, and carry so little overhead.

In a recent development, this design has more than a decade of tooling behind it. Compose, Kubernetes, OCI registries, image scanners, and nearly every CI system treat the container as the common primitive. If the job is to run a service, execute a code snippet, process one request, or run an evaluation and disappear, a container is usually the obvious pick, and it will stay that way.

ⓘ Containers share one kernel, even inside a VM. On macOS and Windows, Docker Desktop runs your Linux containers inside a virtual machine, which keeps them off your host operating system. Every container in that VM still shares its single kernel, so the isolation between one container and the next is unchanged.

In a recent development, docker Sandboxes run an AI coding agent inside a microVM that has its own Linux kernel, its own filesystem and network stack, and a private Docker Engine. The agent gets sudo inside the isolated environment. It can install packages, run services, build images, and bring up an entire Compose application without reaching the host Docker daemon, the host filesystem outside its workspace, or other sandboxes on the same machine.

Getting one running takes a single command, using sbx, the Docker Sandboxes CLI:.

In a recent development, that creates the sandbox and starts the agent. You can stop it, resume it, and come back to everything the agent installed until you remove the sandbox.

Coding agents need a full machine because their sessions build up state over hours and they act on unvetted instructions. A container is built for a process with a known set of dependencies, and an agent’s work doesn’t fit that shape.

An agent needs the authority of a whole machine and a boundary designed for one. The capabilities that make an agent useful, such as running code, installing packages, and reaching the network, are the same ones that wear at the walls around it. An agent probes the edges of its environment because the job requires changing that environment.

Recent findings suggest that A coding agent’s session looks like a developer’s afternoon. It clones a repository, installs packages, starts PostgreSQL, runs migrations, builds images, launches the app with Compose, reads the logs, changes the code, and tries again. That loop can run for hours, and each step depends on what the previous one left behind.

A container is designed to be rebuilt from an image and a few explicit volumes. The packages, databases, and build output an agent creates outside those volumes are lost when the container is recreated. That’s less than ideal for a session where every step builds on the last.

Box by ASCII describes this distinction neatly: “It uses the sandbox the way a developer uses a laptop, so the sandbox has to behave like one.”.

The program deciding which command to run is probabilistic, and it can read instructions from many places at once, including source files, issue descriptions, web pages, package metadata, and MCP tool output. Some of that input is untrusted, and a malicious instruction planted in a README or a tool description can steer the agent on purpose. The code it generates may also be wrong or actively hostile.

According to recent reports, we’ve already seen an agent that deleted a production database after misreading its task. Once the agent is running unattended in YOLO mode, there’s no permission prompt left to catch it. A workload with that much authority and that little predictability needs a boundary designed for it.

Put these facts together and you get the reason why we built Docker Sandboxes. An autonomous coding agent needs machine-shaped capabilities without access to everything on the developer’s machine, which comes down to four things:.

The next sections show what each looks like, starting with containment.

Recent findings suggest that the short version is that a container’s boundary is the host kernel it shares, and Docker Sandboxes have a hypervisor boundary around a kernel the agent has to itself. That one difference decides how far a compromise can travel, and it also settles the awkward question of how an agent could get access to Docker.

This is where containers and containment part ways. A container can be part of containment, and often should be, but containment covers the whole environment around the agent. It starts with a boundary the model can’t rewrite, which is why Docker uses a microVM with its own kernel for autonomous agents.

Industry observers note that A container’s boundary is enforced by the kernel it shares, so escaping it requires a kernel exploit or a side-channel attack. Those aren’t everyday finds. Past that bar, though, sits the entire host kernel, every other process on the machine, and any credentials mounted alongside them.

According to recent reports, ⓘ This scenario is specific to Linux environments. On Docker Desktop (macOS and Windows), the shared kernel is the Docker Desktop VM’s kernel, not the host kernel, so an escape would land in that VM rather than the operating system.

Docker Sandboxes give the agent its own kernel behind a hypervisor boundary. If an agent escapes its container, it lands in a disposable microVM, and the host stays out of reach. And you can delete the sandbox and start another. Each agent also gets its own microVM, so two agents running on the same machine can’t reach each other’s sandboxes either. However, the agent can still reach whatever you chose to share with it, including the workspace, allowed network destinations, MCP servers, and skills.

Mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a container is the long-standing way to give it Docker access, and it turns up in Compose setups, CI pipelines, and observability tools. It also hands the container control of the host Docker daemon, which Docker limits to trusted users because it can mount host paths and start privileged containers.

An agent doesn’t need an exploit to use that. Put one in a container started with the socket mounted, and it probes its surroundings, works out that it’s in a container, and finds the hole in the configuration. In Mark’s keynote demo, that was enough for an agent to reach a secrets file on the host with no zero-day involved.

According to recent reports, the socket is one hole among several, and agents find them because probing their environment is part of the work. Docker-in-Docker, mounted credentials, and broad host mounts are others. Containers were built to isolate an application that behaves as configured. But an agent keeps testing that configuration, so if there’s a gap, it’s likely to find it.

In a recent development, docker Sandboxes put the missing boundary in the right place. The agent talks to a private Docker Engine inside the guest. It can build images, run Testcontainers, and start a whole Compose stack, and the host daemon and its socket stay outside the microVM the entire time. Containers keep doing what they do best, inside a boundary the agent can’t widen.

Recent findings suggest that let’s say you ask an agent running inside Docker Sandboxes to find a secrets file on the host. It’ll find a Docker socket, try to use it to mount host paths and start privileged containers, but won’t reach the host. A microVM can give it a much stronger trust boundary than a container. The architecture behind Docker Sandboxes goes deeper on why a microVM was the right shape for this.

Containment draws the boundary. Control is what you can see and stop inside it: what the agent is allowed to reach, and the ability to block it when it heads somewhere it shouldn’t. In a sandbox, those controls are enforced by the host, outside the agent’s reach, so the agent can’t switch them off or reason its way around them. Outbound traffic, credentials, and organization-wide policy all work this way. Control also means knowing what the agent can still touch, because a microVM can’t hide what you choose to share with it.

Runs its own Linux kernel in a microVM.

Needs the host socket or a nested daemon.

Uses a private Docker Engine inside the microVM.

Uses a direct read-write mount or an in-VM private clone.

Uses the container network and whatever controls its operator supplies.

Sends outbound traffic through a host proxy with deny-by-default policy.

Commonly receives environment variables, files, or mounted sockets.

Uses host-side credential injection for supported HTTP services.

Usually rebuilt from an image and explicit volumes.

Keeps packages, images, containers, and agent history until sbx rm.

Fits Compose, Kubernetes, and most CI systems.

Uses the sbx lifecycle and experimental environment files.

These controls hold because they run outside the agent process. A rule the agent can reach is a rule it can work around, so the rules that matter live on the host. Outbound traffic goes through a host-side proxy with a deny-by-default policy, which means a destination the agent wants stays blocked until someone adds it to the list. Credentials follow the same logic. For supported HTTP services, the proxy injects them into outbound requests, so the agent can use a credential without the raw value ever entering the VM.

When one developer’s setup needs to become a team standard, Docker AI Governance can move network, filesystem, and MCP policy into organization-wide controls.

A microVM can’t hide what you choose to share with it, so the shared parts deserve the most attention.

It has been revealed that the workspace is the largest of them. It’s mounted read-write by default, so the agent can edit or delete files in your project. Clone mode gives the agent a private in-VM clone to work in, which protects the host working tree, though the original repository stays readable inside the sandbox.

MCP servers and skills are shared too. A local stdio MCP server runs on the host and shared agent skills use a host-side store, so the agent’s reach extends to both.

So whichever mode you pick, be sure to read the diff before you run modified code.

In a recent development, docker Sandboxes may cost some configuration and a supported hypervisor. But Kits and environment files account for the configuration, and they’re also where you get choice over agents and tools and the capacity to reproduce a setup across a team.

Sources indicate that kits make setup repeatable by packaging tools, files, commands, network rules, credentials, and agent instructions. They’re published for different agents, tools, and IDEs, so you can swap what runs inside the sandbox without rebuilding the environment around it. An sbxenv.yaml file records one project’s sandbox configuration, and committing it to the repo lets a teammate recreate the same sandbox with one command, so every developer works from the same setup. (Kits are in early access and environment files are experimental, so strategy for changes to both.).

The host-enforced controls take some setup too. Network policy requires someone to decide which destinations belong in the workflow, credential mediation adds service bindings and approved domains, and clone mode adds a fetch step before changes land in the host repository.

According to recent reports, running a sandbox takes more from your machine than running a container does. It needs a supported hypervisor, which today means Apple silicon on macOS 14 or later, Windows Hypervisor Platform, or KVM on supported Ubuntu systems, and running inside another VM requires nested virtualization. The separate kernel and Docker Engine also consume more memory and disk than one additional container would.

Recent findings suggest that if your machine is the limiting factor, Docker Cloud Sandboxes run the same microVM isolation on Docker-managed compute, and one command moves a sandbox between your laptop and the cloud. Local and cloud sandboxes keep separate secrets and network policies.

Choose a container when you control the code and its dependencies, and choose Docker Sandboxes when the workload generates or fetches code at runtime and needs its own boundary.

Reach for Docker Sandboxes when.

You control the code and its dependencies.

The workload generates or fetches code at runtime.

Execution is short-lived and rebuilt from an image.

The session accumulates state for hours.

The workload doesn’t need Docker, or runs in CI that already provides it.

The workload needs its own Docker Engine with no path to the host socket.

You want maximum density and a fit with Compose or Kubernetes.

You need host-enforced network and credential policy the workload can’t switch off.

The kernel boundary is enough for the code you’re running.

You want a hypervisor between the workload and your kernel.

If any of the signals below apply to your project, you should start with Docker Sandboxes.

Start with sbx run claude. Add clone mode, kits, network policy, credential mediation, and organization governance as your workflow grows.

Containers aren’t going anywhere. For services, CI jobs, and anything you package to ship, they draw the right boundary, and the ecosystem around them is the reason they’ll keep doing that work. A coding agent needs more than a container to be trusted with real work. It needs containment, meaning a boundary the model can’t rewrite, controls it can’t reason its way around, and the freedom to choose its tools and scale its setup.

Docker Sandboxes provide that containment in a microVM that can still run your containers. The boundary is also what lets the agent move faster. With it in place, you can stop approving every command and let the agent get to work. Once one developer’s setup needs to become a team standard, Docker AI Governance extends the same controls across your organization.

In a recent development, give it a try and get a sandbox running with one command. Start with sbx run claude and the Docker Sandboxes quickstart.
